fields.description:
Streams groups support broker-side custom task assignors. A custom implementation
may return an invalid assignment, but the coordinator currently does not validate several assignment invariants before accepting the result.

No issue has been identified in the built-in sticky assignor. This proposal adds validation to detect invalid output from faulty custom assignors and provide a clear error before that output becomes the group's target assignment.

For example:
 # Member A currently owns task T as active.
 # A custom assignor returns T as active for both A and member B.
 # The coordinator accepts both target assignments.
 # A retains T because it remains in its target assignment.
 # B waits for A to release T.

While A retains ownership and the conflicting target remains unchanged, B cannot
complete reconciliation. The coordinator does not report the invalid assignor
output as the cause.
fields.summary: Validate Streams task assignor output before accepting target assignments

fields.description:
h2. Summary

With {{{}group.protocol=streams{}}}, {{StreamThread}} rebuilds the task offset sum snapshot on every processing loop iteration, even when the offsets and task states have not changed. This performs task enumeration, map copying, filtering, and allocation independently of whether the next heartbeat will report new offsets.

A local JMH benchmark shows that the cost of one refresh grows approximately linearly with task count. In a separate 10-minute application profile, this path accounted for *580 of 1,207 Java execution samples (48.1%)* from the Streams processing thread, including descendant calls.
h2. Current behavior

{{TaskManager.maybeUpdateTaskOffsetSumSnapshot()}} performs the following work:
 # Copies the process-wide local offset map from {{{}StateDirectory{}}}.
 # Builds a map of this thread's tasks through {{{}allTasks(){}}}, including tasks held by the state updater and tasks awaiting initialization.
 # Removes running active tasks and overlays live changelog offset sums for other eligible tasks.
 # Builds a separate map with heartbeat task IDs and publishes a read-only snapshot.

The snapshot is refreshed on each loop iteration in both processing-loop variants. Heartbeat code separately checks assignment changes, the offset reporting interval, warm-up progress, and whether the values changed. These checks limit offset transmission but do not avoid the preceding snapshot construction.

The copied local offset map is in memory; this path does not read task state from disk on every iteration. Under {{{}group.protocol=classic{}}}, this snapshot refresh method returns immediately; classic reports offset sums through its subscription metadata path.
h2. Environment
 * Kafka {{{}4.5.0-SNAPSHOT{}}}, checkout {{{}e0b738a78819d95dd7779ec3d98effbb9f6a0f9c{}}}.
 * macOS AArch64; JFR reports 14 hardware threads.
 * JMH: JMH 1.37, JDK 25.0.3.
 * Application profile: JDK 21.0.5+11-LTS.
 * Affected released versions have not been established.

h2. JMH results

{{TaskOffsetSumSnapshotBenchmark.refreshSnapshot}} measures one refresh with unchanged offsets. All tasks belong to one stream thread and each has one changelog partition.

The fixture uses the real task manager, task registry, state manager, state updater, and local offset map. It does not start a broker or perform disk I/O. RUNNING tasks are registered as active tasks and produce an empty final snapshot. RESTORING tasks remain in the state updater input queue; the updater thread is not started.

Settings: one worker, three forks, {{{}-Xms2g -Xmx2g{}}}, five 2-second warmup iterations and five 2-second measurement iterations per fork, {{{}avgt{}}}, and {{{}-prof gc{}}}. There are 15 measurements per parameter combination. Time errors below are the JMH 99.9% confidence interval half-widths.
||Task count||Task state||Time (us/op, mean ± error)||Allocation (B/op)||
|0|RUNNING|0.257 ± 0.002|2,120.001|
|0|RESTORING|0.259 ± 0.001|2,120.001|
|100|RUNNING|8.481 ± 0.057|31,890.708|
|100|RESTORING|22.821 ± 0.111|77,048.131|
|1,000|RUNNING|89.110 ± 1.960|346,829.769|
|1,000|RESTORING|248.191 ± 1.702|831,546.901|
|5,000|RUNNING|429.778 ± 5.789|1,732,682.127|
|5,000|RESTORING|1,304.563 ± 22.457|4,111,075.094|

The RUNNING cases show that copying and filtering still incur a cost when all local entries are excluded from the final snapshot. Allocation is measured per refresh, not retained heap size.

The results were collected in two runs: task count 1,000, and task counts 0/100/5,000. For example, the latter used:
{code:bash}
java -jar jmh-benchmarks/build/libs/kafka-jmh-benchmarks-4.5.0-SNAPSHOT-all.jar \
  TaskOffsetSumSnapshotBenchmark \
  -p taskCount=0,100,5000 -p taskState=RUNNING,RESTORING \
  -f 3 -wi 5 -i 5 -w 2s -r 2s \
  -prof gc -foe true \
  -rf json -rff jmh-benchmarks/build/task-offset-snapshot-scaling.json
{code}
Benchmark source: [^TaskOffsetSumSnapshotBenchmark.java]
Raw results: [^task-offset-snapshot-1000.json], [^task-offset-snapshot-scaling.json]
h2. Application profile and flame graph

The application uses one sub-topology:
{noformat}
snapshot-bench-input
  -> groupByKey()
  -> count(persistent key-value store)
{noformat}
The configured test uses {{{}group.protocol=streams{}}}, {{{}num.stream.threads=1{}}}, and {{{}poll.ms=10{}}}. JFR was recorded with {{{}settings=profile{}}}, a 60-second start delay, and a 600-second duration. The intended workload was 100 tasks with no continuous input; the exact assigned task count and input activity during this recording were not independently captured.

The recording contains 1,225 {{jdk.ExecutionSample}} events, including 1,207 from {{{}StreamThread-1{}}}. The flame graph uses these Java execution events only. Native-method, allocation, and waiting events are excluded; none of the recorded execution stacks are marked truncated.
||Processing-thread call path, including descendants||Samples||Share of 1,207 samples||
|TaskManager.maybeUpdateTaskOffsetSumSnapshot|580|48.1%|
|TaskManager.process|255|21.1%|
|StreamThread.maybeCommit|157|13.0%|
|TaskManager.recordTaskProcessRatio|128|10.6%|
|TaskManager.punctuate|39|3.2%|
|pollPhase and other paths|48|4.0%|

The {{process}} and {{maybeCommit}} paths include readiness checks; their presence does not establish that records were processed or commits completed.

Within the 580 snapshot-path samples, the sampled call sites were:
||Snapshot operation||Samples||
|allTasks() and task iteration preparation|284|
|Copying the StateDirectory offset map|194|
|Removing running active tasks from the copied map|98|
|Other|4|

Descendant frames include {{{}TaskId.hashCode(){}}}, {{HashMap}} insertion/removal, {{ConcurrentHashMap}} traversal, and state-updater task enumeration.

*48.1% is a share of Java execution samples, not whole-process CPU utilization or the fraction of a CPU core consumed.*

Separately, cumulative thread CPU counters in the first and last recorded thread dumps increased by 63.956 seconds over 543.632 seconds of elapsed time for the Streams processing thread. This corresponds to approximately *11.8% of one CPU core* over that interval. The sample share does not establish an exact CPU time or potential saving for the snapshot method.

Flame graphs: [^stream-thread.svg], [^all-java.svg]. Download and open the SVG in a browser to zoom and search for {{{}maybeUpdateTaskOffsetSumSnapshot{}}}.
h2. Interpretation and limits

The microbenchmark demonstrates repeated work with unchanged inputs, and the application profile identifies snapshot construction as a prominent Java execution path in the measured run.

An earlier 120-second recording with {{poll.ms=100}} contained only 27 Java execution samples and no snapshot-path samples. It is too sparse to establish the snapshot's CPU share. The application ID also changed between runs, and task/input conditions were not fully recorded, so these profiles are not a controlled comparison of poll intervals.

The JMH and application runs used different JDK versions. No production throughput regression, lock contention bottleneck, or measured improvement is established by these results.
fields.summary: Repeated task offset snapshot rebuilding adds overhead with the Streams rebalance protocol

comments.body:
[~mjsax] [~lucasbru] 

Sorry for pinging you out of the blue.

If this problem should be addressed, I think it would be better to calculate and send the offset only when sending a heartbeat.
My understanding is that the offset is only needed at that point for now, and doing so could reduce CPU usage caused by unnecessarily creating snapshots.

Alternatively, I think it would also be fine to send a slightly stale offset in the heartbeat.
Even with the current implementation, the offset snapshot sent by the client does not necessarily represent the most up-to-date offset.

What do you think?

Sounds valid. We haven't really measured a difference in our regression benchmarks, so I assume it's not so bad, but it's for sure not ideal.

A useful improvement would probably be to throttle the updates in state updater and stream thread to hearbeatIntervalMs / 5 for example, and possibly force-rebuilding at specific events (onTasksAssigned / onTasksRevoked / onAllTasksLost). 

wdyt?

A local JMH benchmark shows that the cost of one refresh grows approximately linearly with task count. In a separate 10-minute application profile, this path accounted for 580 of 1,207 Java execution samples (48.1%) from the Streams processing thread, including descendant calls.

Current behavior

TaskManager.maybeUpdateTaskOffsetSumSnapshot() performs the following work:

  1. Copies the process-wide local offset map from StateDirectory.
  2. Builds a map of this thread's tasks through allTasks(), including tasks held by the state updater and tasks awaiting initialization.
  3. Removes running active tasks and overlays live changelog offset sums for other eligible tasks.
  4. Builds a separate map with heartbeat task IDs and publishes a read-only snapshot.

The snapshot is refreshed on each loop iteration in both processing-loop variants. Heartbeat code separately checks assignment changes, the offset reporting interval, warm-up progress, and whether the values changed. The copied local offset map is in memory; this path does not read task state from disk on every iteration. Under group.protocol=classic, this snapshot refresh method returns immediately; classic reports offset sums through its subscription metadata path.

fields.summary: Flaky StreamsUpgradeTest.test_app_upgrade: window changelogs are deleted by retention before restore

renderedFields.description:
The trunk SmokeTestDriver writes records two days in the past, but the old smoke-test clients create their window changelogs with only about one day of retention, so the broker deletes data the clients still need. After the upgrade, the checkpoints point to deleted offsets, the tasks are marked as corrupted and restored again and again, and the clients start too slowly, so the test times out.

The data loss happens in every run; StreamsUpgradeTest.test_app_upgrade fails only when the extra restores take longer than 60 s:

TimeoutError: Did expect to read 'SMOKE-TEST-CLIENT-STARTED' from ducker@ducker51

Why the retention is too short:

  • apache/kafka#18830 moved the driver timestamps two days into the past and set windowstore.changelog.additional.retention.ms to three days in SmokeTestClient, but not in the old copies in streams/upgrade-system-tests-XY, which use the default of one day.
  • The old client creates the changelogs, e.g. SmokeTest-KSTREAM-REDUCE-STATE-STORE-0000000020-changelog with retention.ms=86432000. Changelog records keep the two-day-old input timestamps, so the broker deletes them almost right away.
  • Streams does not change the config of an existing internal topic, so the topic keeps this retention after the upgrade.

Seen with from_version 4.0.1, 4.1.2 and 3.9.2. The attached logs (test_app_upgrade-from-4.0.1-failed-logs.tar.gz) are from a failed 4.0.1 run; see 537/StreamsSmokeTestJobRunnerService-0-*/ducker51/streams.log and the broker server-start-stdout-stderr.log files.

For example, this is one changelog partition of the failed client in the attached logs (ducker51/streams.log, client id and stack traces removed). The broker had already moved the log start offset of this partition to 61:

06:03:01,325 stream-task [0_2] State store KSTREAM-REDUCE-STATE-STORE-0000000020 initialized from checkpoint with offset 8 at changelog ...-changelog-2
06:03:01,347 Seeking to offset 9 for partition ...-changelog-2
06:03:01,530 WARN Encountered OffsetOutOfRangeException fetching records from restore consumer for partitions [...-changelog-2] ... marking the corresponding tasks as corrupted and re-initializing it later.
06:03:07,289 ERROR Get exceptions for the following tasks: {0_2=TaskCorruptedException: Tasks [0_2] are corrupted and hence need to be re-initialized}
06:03:10,423 stream-task [0_2] State store KSTREAM-REDUCE-STATE-STORE-0000000020 did not find checkpoint offset, hence would default to the starting offset at changelog ...-changelog-2
06:03:11,599 Seeking to offset 60 for partition ...-changelog-2
06:03:11,605 WARN Failed to seek by timestamp for changelog partitions [...-changelog-2], falling back to seek-to-beginning

The task first tries to restore from its checkpoint (offset 9, already deleted), is marked as corrupted and re-initialized, then fails again at offset 60 before it restores from the beginning. Partitions 1 and 4 of the same client also failed to restore from their checkpoints (offsets 78 and 39) and were re-initialized.

To reproduce (the test often passes, so look for the data loss in the logs):

TC_PATHS="tests/kafkatest/tests/streams/streams_application_upgrade_test.py::StreamsUpgradeTest.test_app_upgrade@'{\"from_version\":\"4.0.1\",\"metadata_quorum\":\"COMBINED_KRAFT\"}'" _DUCKTAPE_OPTIONS="--repeat 5" tests/docker/run_tests.sh

grep -rl "OffsetOutOfRangeException" --include="streams.log*" results/latest

fields.description:
We've seen the snappy-java CVEs 
 * CVE-2026-93452 ([snappy issue|https://github.com/xerial/snappy-java/issues/732])
 * CVE-2026-90559 ([snappy issue|https://github.com/xerial/snappy-java/issues/728])
 * CVE-2026-93451 ([snappy issue|https://github.com/xerial/snappy-java/issues/729])

Unfortunately, the snappy-java community seems to be not maintained anymore. 

Moreover, the is [lz4-jave community|https://github.com/lz4/lz4-java] is not maintained anymore, either. Currently, we use the [forked repo|https://github.com/yawkat/lz4-java] created by a user (yawkat). The single user repository might enter the unmaintained state anytime.

 

proposal:

To improve that, we can create a config to allow kafka admin to disable some compression methods when written. This way, we can avoid the bad users to attack kafka using these impacted compression methods.

Note: we cannot get rid of these compression methods because the history log in kafka will not be able to be decompressed anymore.
fields.summary: Allow kafka admin to disable some compression methods

fields.description:
The broker-side Streams assignor API exposes client rack information, but does not expose the topic partitions associated with each task or the racks hosting their replicas. Although this metadata is available on the broker, custom assignors cannot use it through the current API to make locality-aware assignment decisions.

When partition replicas are available only in a subset of racks, assigning a task to a client outside those racks can introduce avoidable cross-rack traffic. Depending on the deployment topology, this may increase read latency and network costs.

Classic Streams already supports this optimization through KIP-925, balancing partition locality against task distribution and assignment stability. KIP-1071 also explicitly identifies KIP-925-style optimization as future work for the Streams rebalance protocol.

We should close this gap by making the necessary partition and replica rack metadata available to broker-side Streams assignors and supporting locality-aware assignment. The initial scope can focus on active tasks and their input partitions, while preserving balanced task distribution and avoiding unnecessary task movement.

Validation should cover deployments where replicas do not span all client racks, missing rack information, and the trade-off between locality improvements and task movement. Actual traffic reduction should be evaluated with rack-aware fetching configured appropriately.
fields.summary: Support rack-aware task assignment in the Streams group protocol in terms of partition rack

comments.body: Hi, this ticket looks related to two tickets I'm working on: KAFKA-20999 (KIP-708 tag-based standby placement for the streams group protocol, PR coming soon) and its follow-up KAFKA-16867 (using client.rack as an implicit tag). I think the goals are different, yours is active-task locality and mine is standby spreading, but we'd both be changing StickyTaskAssignor and the rack-related metadata. Could you take a look at those two and we can sync on scope so we don't step on each other?

Based on the learning from KIP-1071 implementation, I am not sure if we should really support KIP-925 with "streams" protocol. The implemented algorithm are rather compute expensive and putting this type of load on the group-coordinator might not be a good thing.

I am actually not even sure, how many people use/rely on KIP-925... Before we pick up this work, I would like to get broader user feedback that there is high demand for it. Otherwise, it might not be worth doing it.

fields.description:
*Description*

Processing costs can vary across stages within a Kafka Streams topology. Simple filtering or transformation may require relatively little CPU, while complex aggregations or windowed operations may require more processing resources. As a result, assigning an equal number of tasks to each instance does not necessarily produce a balanced workload.

Automatically measuring these differences at runtime and incorporating them into assignment decisions on the client or broker is challenging. Observed load depends on input traffic and the execution environment, and temporary traffic spikes need to be distinguished from sustained differences in processing cost. Reassigning tasks in response to short-lived fluctuations may introduce unnecessary task movement and state restoration costs.

Application developers and operators, however, may understand the relative processing costs through knowledge of the application logic and experience from long-term monitoring. It would be useful to express this knowledge as user-defined weights and incorporate them into task assignment.

 

*Proposal*

Allow users to specify relative processing weights through the builder APIs used to construct a topology, or a similar mechanism, and make these weights available to the task assignor.

For example, users could assign a lower weight to a simple filtering stage and a higher weight to a complex aggregation or windowed operation. The weights would represent relative estimated processing costs, rather than execution priorities. Individual tasks would remain the unit of assignment.

The granularity and API for declaring weights, how weights from multiple processing stages contribute to a task’s estimated cost, how this information is passed to the assignor, and its interaction with existing assignment policies would be discussed in a KIP.
fields.summary: Support user-defined processing weights for Kafka Streams task assignment

comments.body:
When using Kafka Streams, I have occasionally encountered situations where a particular task required significantly more resources than others, which could make the node hosting that task unstable.

This made me wonder whether it might be useful to allow users to assign a weight to each task and have the task assignor take those weights into account so that the workload can be distributed more evenly across instances. If this idea sounds reasonable, I would be interested in writing a KIP and discussing it further with the community.

fields.description:
When a broker loses leadership of a __transaction_state partition, there is a *race* between the replica state change and the transaction coordinator's resignation. BrokerMetadataPublisher.onMetadataUpdate applies the delta to ReplicaManager first, which makes the broker a follower. It then updates the group coordinator, and only after that calls TransactionCoordinator.onResignation, which drops the partition's entry from the TransactionStateManager cache. Until resignation runs, the broker is a follower for the partition but still answers coordinator requests from its old cache. The window is usually short, but its length depends on how much work the publish does before it reaches the transaction coordinator, and it can stretch to seconds.

TransactionStateManager.getAndMaybeAddTransactionState only checks loadingPartitions and transactionMetadataCache; it never checks that the broker still leads the partition. Answers that require a log write are safe: the acks=-1 append fails with NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER, which is mapped to NOT_COORDINATOR. Answers decided purely from the cache are not, so any request that hits the old coordinator inside the window can get a wrong answer.

{*}With TV2{*}, one way to lose this race is a fatal producer error:
1. Transaction N commits on coordinator A. A's cache holds COMPLETE_COMMIT at epoch E, and the client now has epoch E.
2. Leadership of the __transaction_state partition moves to broker B. B loads the partition, and the partition leaders' implicit AddPartitionsToTxn for transaction N+1 go to B, which moves the transaction to ONGOING.
3. The client has had no reason to rediscover the coordinator: under TV2, EndTxn is its first coordinator request in the transaction. So it sends EndTxn(COMMIT, E) to A.
4. If this request reaches A after A became a follower but before it resigned, A answers from its cache. COMPLETE_COMMIT + COMMIT at the current epoch is not a retry, so A returns INVALID_TXN_STATE without writing to the log:
TransactionalId: <id>'s state is COMPLETE_COMMIT, but received transaction marker result to send: COMMIT
5. The producer treats INVALID_TXN_STATE as fatal. The transaction on B stays ONGOING until it times out (or the producer re-initializes).

If the EndTxn arrives after A resigns, A returns NOT_COORDINATOR, and the client rediscovers B and commits normally. The outcome depends only on which side of that window the request lands. It doesn't need a broker pause or any fault: an ordinary leadership move (reassignment, controlled shutdown, preferred leader election) is enough, and producers that commit often are the most exposed.

Other answers decided purely from the cache race the same way, for example PRODUCER_FENCED / INVALID_PRODUCER_ID_MAPPING, the verify-only AddPartitionsToTxn path, and the "partitions already added" shortcut.

items.fromString:
When a broker loses leadership of a __transaction_state partition, its TransactionStateManager keeps the partition's cache entry until TransactionCoordinator.onResignation runs. In BrokerMetadataPublisher.onMetadataUpdate, that happens after replicaManager.applyDelta and after the group coordinator update. So there's a window in which the broker is already a follower for the partition but still answers coordinator requests from its old cache.

TransactionStateManager.getAndMaybeAddTransactionState (trunk lines 400-421) only checks loadingPartitions and transactionMetadataCache; it never checks that the broker still leads the partition. Answers that require a log write are safe, because the acks=-1 append fails with NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER, which is mapped to NOT_COORDINATOR. Answers decided purely from the cache are not.

With TV2 this surfaces as a fatal error for the producer:
1. Transaction N commits on coordinator A. The cache on A holds COMPLETE_COMMIT at epoch E, and the client now has epoch E.
2. Leadership of the __transaction_state partition moves to broker B. B loads the partition, and the partition leaders' implicit AddPartitionsToTxn for transaction N+1 go to B, which moves the transaction to ONGOING.
3. The client hasn't had any reason to rediscover the coordinator: under TV2 its first coordinator request in the transaction is EndTxn. So it sends EndTxn(COMMIT, E) to A.
4. A is already a follower but hasn't resigned yet. It answers from the cache: COMPLETE_COMMIT + COMMIT at the current epoch is not a retry, so it returns INVALID_TXN_STATE without writing to the log:
TransactionalId: <id>'s state is COMPLETE_COMMIT, but received transaction marker result to send: COMMIT
5. The producer treats INVALID_TXN_STATE as fatal. The transaction on B stays ONGOING until it times out.

The correct response is NOT_COORDINATOR, which would make the client rediscover B and commit. We've seen gaps of several seconds between the broker becoming follower and resigning, and in one case ~37 s, with no broker pause involved.

Other cache-only answers are exposed the same way, for example PRODUCER_FENCED / INVALID_PRODUCER_ID_MAPPING, the verify-only AddPartitionsToTxn path, and the "partitions already added" shortcut.

It then updates the group coordinator, and only after that calls TransactionCoordinator.onResignation, which drops the partition's entry from the TransactionStateManager cache. Until resignation runs, the broker is a follower for the partition but still answers coordinator requests from its old cache. The window is usually short, but its length depends on how much work the publish does before it reaches the transaction coordinator, and it can stretch to seconds.

TransactionStateManager.getAndMaybeAddTransactionState only checks loadingPartitions and transactionMetadataCache; it never checks that the broker still leads the partition. Answers that require a log write are safe: the acks=-1 append fails with NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER, which is mapped to NOT_COORDINATOR. Answers decided purely from the cache are not, so any request that hits the old coordinator inside the window can get a wrong answer.

{*}With TV2{*}, one way to lose this race is a fatal producer error:
1. Transaction N commits on coordinator A. A's cache holds COMPLETE_COMMIT at epoch E, and the client now has epoch E.
2. Leadership of the __transaction_state partition moves to broker B. B loads the partition, and the partition leaders' implicit AddPartitionsToTxn for transaction N+1 go to B, which moves the transaction to ONGOING.
3. The client has had no reason to rediscover the coordinator: under TV2, EndTxn is its first coordinator request in the transaction. So it sends EndTxn(COMMIT, E) to A.
4. If this request reaches A after A became a follower but before it resigned, A answers from its cache. COMPLETE_COMMIT + COMMIT at the current epoch is not a retry, so A returns INVALID_TXN_STATE without writing to the log:
TransactionalId: <id>'s state is COMPLETE_COMMIT, but received transaction marker result to send: COMMIT
5. The producer treats INVALID_TXN_STATE as fatal. The transaction on B stays ONGOING until it times out (or the producer re-initializes).

If the EndTxn arrives after A resigns, A returns NOT_COORDINATOR, and the client rediscovers B and commits normally. The outcome depends only on which side of that window the request lands. It doesn't need a broker pause or any fault: an ordinary leadership move (reassignment, controlled shutdown, preferred leader election) is enough, and producers that commit often are the most exposed.

Other answers decided purely from the cache race the same way, for example PRODUCER_FENCED / INVALID_PRODUCER_ID_MAPPING, the verify-only AddPartitionsToTxn path, and the "partitions already added" shortcut.

fields.description:
The Assignment field in StreamsGroupDescribe currently includes only assignedTasks, excluding tasks in tasksPendingRevocation. However, the coordinator still considers the member responsible for these tasks until revocation is acknowledged.

When an active task moves from member A to member B, it can therefore disappear from both members’ current assignments in the Describe response: A is still pending revocation, while B cannot receive the task until A releases it. This makes it difficult to identify which member is holding up the transfer.

The same issue was fixed for consumer groups in KAFKA-20431. We should similarly include tasks pending revocation in the assignment returned by StreamsGroupDescribe, covering active, standby, and warm-up tasks.

fields.description:
*Background*

KIP-1071 defines rules that Streams task assignments must satisfy. For example, the same stateful task must not be assigned to different members sharing the same processId, even in different roles such as active and standby.

With KIP-1357 enabling broker-side custom assignors, developers would benefit from an easy way to verify these rules in their unit tests. Shared test utilities would reduce the risk of developers overlooking or interpreting rules differently when writing their own validation code.

 

*Proposal*

Provide shared test utilities that custom assignor developers can use in their own tests.

Developers should be able to construct test inputs, run their assignor, and pass the inputs and resulting assignment to the utilities to check compliance with assignment rules. When a rule is violated, the utilities should identify the affected tasks and members and explain the violation.

The checks should be based on KIP-1071’s requirements and aligned with the active and standby assignment responsibilities of custom assignors under the current public API. This would help developers test the constraints required by the Streams protocol while implementing their own assignment policies.

fields.description:
*Description*

ConsumerGroup.validateOffsetCommit() looks up the member by memberId without first validating the current owner of groupInstanceId.

When static member A is replaced by member B using the same instance ID, A’s member ID is removed. A subsequent non-transactional OffsetCommit from A therefore receives UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID instead of FENCED_INSTANCE_ID.

Under the same conditions, OffsetCommit in a ClassicGroup and classic Heartbeat in a ConsumerGroup return FENCED_INSTANCE_ID.

*Impact*

Upon receiving UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID from OffsetCommit, the classic client clears its member ID and requests to rejoin. A rejoin request with an empty member ID and the same instance ID can replace the current static member B again.

Heartbeat fencing does not always prevent this. If the commit error resets the generation first, a delayed fencing heartbeat response for the previous generation can be ignored as stale.

*Expected Behavior*

For replaced classic static members in a ConsumerGroup, OffsetCommit should preserve the existing static membership fencing behavior and return FENCED_INSTANCE_ID.

 

*NOTE*

{{ConsumerGroup.validateOffsetCommit()}} also handles members using the new consumer protocol. The new client’s commit response handler has no dedicated handling for {{{}FENCED_INSTANCE_ID{}}}, so any additional validation must consider compatibility with both protocols.

fields.summary: Merging topics with different partition counts leaves some records unprocessed under the Streams Rebalance Protocol

comments.body:
Hi [~chickenchickenlove] , thanks for reporting this!

Are you planning to work on a fix, or would you mind if I took it on?

renderedFields.description:
With group.protocol=streams, merging two topics with different partition counts includes nonexistent partitions in the tasks’ inputs, leaving some records unprocessed.

Steps to Reproduce

1. Create topic A with 1 partition(0) and topic B with 3 partitions(0, 1, 2).
2. Run the following topology with group.protocol=streams:

KStream<String, String> streamA = builder.stream("A");
KStream<String, String> streamB = builder.stream("B");

streamA.merge(streamB).to("output");

3. Produce records to A-0, B-0, B-1, and B-2.

  • Expected: All input records appear in `output`.
  • Actual: Records from `B-1` and `B-2` do not appear in `output`, and the following messages repeatedly reference nonexistent partitions:
Requesting the log end offset for A-1 in order to compute lag
Requesting the log end offset for A-2 in order to compute lag

 

Cause

StreamsMembershipManager#topicPartitionsForActiveTasks and DefaultStreamsRebalanceListener#toTopicPartitions apply the task’s partition ID to every input topic without checking each topic’s partition count.

As a result, a task that should include only B-1 also includes A-1. The same issue occurs for partition ID 2.

The classic protocol’s PartitionGrouper checks each topic’s partition count and includes only existing partitions. The new protocol’s conversion paths need equivalent handling.

comments.body:
For the reproducing,

public static void main(String[] args) {

    final Properties props = new Properties();
    props.put(StreamsConfig.APPLICATION_ID_CONFIG, "ASH-HELLO1111100");
    props.put(StreamsConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "localhost:9092");
    props.put(StreamsConfig.GROUP_PROTOCOL_CONFIG, "streams");
    props.put(StreamsConfig.NUM_STREAM_THREADS_CONFIG, 1);
    props.put(StreamsConfig.POLL_MS_CONFIG, 10);
    props.put(StreamsConfig.REPLICATION_FACTOR_CONFIG, 1);
    props.put(StreamsConfig.DEFAULT_KEY_SERDE_CLASS_CONFIG, Serdes.String().getClass().getName());
    props.put(StreamsConfig.DEFAULT_VALUE_SERDE_CLASS_CONFIG, Serdes.String().getClass().getName());
    props.put(ConsumerConfig.AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG, "earliest");


    final StreamsBuilder builder = new StreamsBuilder();

    KStream<Object, Object> streamA = builder.stream("A");
    KStream<Object, Object> streamB = builder.stream("B");
    
    streamA.merge(streamB).to("output");

    final Topology topology = builder.build();
    System.out.println(topology.describe());

    final KafkaStreams kafkaStreams = new KafkaStreams(topology, props);
    Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(kafkaStreams::close));
    kafkaStreams.start();
}

Use this scripts to create topics.

$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic A --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic B --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1

Use this scripts to get output from broker.

$ kcat -b localhost:9092 -C -t output -o beginning -f '%s\n'

Use this scripts to producer messages.

$ printf 'probe1-from-B-1\n' | kcat -b localhost:9092 -P -t B -p 1

Then, there is no observed record at all from "output" topic.

fields.description:
h3. Problem

With {{{}follower.fetch.last.tiered.offset.enable=true{}}}, an empty follower can select a fetch start offset that equals the leader's log start offset. In that case the remote range to rebuild auxiliary state from, [logStartOffset, fetchStartOffset), is empty.

{{TierStateMachine.buildRemoteLogAuxState}} still looks up remote segment metadata for {{{}fetchStartOffset - 1{}}}. That offset is below the log start offset, and its remote log segment may already be deleted, so the lookup can return empty. When it does, the follower fails with {{{}RemoteStorageException{}}}, retries, and stays out of the ISR until the selected offset changes (for example, after the next segment upload). On a low-volume topic this can take a long time.
h3. Observed on 4.3.0

We rebuilt a follower on an empty disk. The selected fetch start offset and the leader's log start offset were both 18203:
{noformat}
ERROR [ReplicaFetcher replicaId=0, leaderId=7, fetcherId=0] Error getting offset for partition <TOPIC-PARTITION>
org.apache.kafka.server.log.remote.storage.RemoteStorageException: Couldn't build the state from remote store for partition: <TOPIC-PARTITION>, currentLeaderEpoch: 406, leaderLocalLogStartOffset: 18203, leaderLogStartOffset: 18203, epoch: 405 as the previous remote log segment metadata was not found
    at kafka.server.TierStateMachine.buildRemoteStorageException(TierStateMachine.java:278)
    at kafka.server.TierStateMachine.lambda$buildRemoteLogAuxState$0(TierStateMachine.java:237)
    at java.base/java.util.Optional.orElseThrow(Optional.java:403)
    at kafka.server.TierStateMachine.buildRemoteLogAuxState(TierStateMachine.java:237)
    at kafka.server.TierStateMachine.start(TierStateMachine.java:113)

fields.summary: Empty follower fails to start when the KIP-1023 fetch start offset equals the leader's log start offset

renderedFields.description:
Problem

With follower.fetch.last.tiered.offset.enable=true, an empty follower can select a fetch start offset that equals the leader's log start offset. In that case the remote range to rebuild auxiliary state from, [logStartOffset, fetchStartOffset), is empty.

TierStateMachine.buildRemoteLogAuxState still looks up remote segment metadata for fetchStartOffset - 1. That offset is below the log start offset, and its remote log segment may already be deleted, so the lookup can return empty. When it does, the follower fails with RemoteStorageException, retries, and stays out of the ISR until the selected offset changes (for example, after the next segment upload). On a low-volume topic this can take a long time.

Observed on 4.3.0

We rebuilt a follower on an empty disk. The selected fetch start offset and the leader's log start offset were both 18203:

ERROR [ReplicaFetcher replicaId=0, leaderId=7, fetcherId=0] Error getting offset for partition <TOPIC-PARTITION>
org.apache.kafka.server.log.remote.storage.RemoteStorageException: Couldn't build the state from remote store for partition: <TOPIC-PARTITION>, currentLeaderEpoch: 406, leaderLocalLogStartOffset: 18203, leaderLogStartOffset: 18203, epoch: 405 as the previous remote log segment metadata was not found
    at kafka.server.TierStateMachine.buildRemoteStorageException(TierStateMachine.java:278)
    at kafka.server.TierStateMachine.lambda$buildRemoteLogAuxState$0(TierStateMachine.java:237)
    at java.base/java.util.Optional.orElseThrow(Optional.java:403)
    at kafka.server.TierStateMachine.buildRemoteLogAuxState(TierStateMachine.java:237)
    at kafka.server.TierStateMachine.start(TierStateMachine.java:113)
    at kafka.server.AbstractFetcherThread.fetchOffsetAndTruncate(AbstractFetcherThread.scala:679)
    at kafka.server.AbstractFetcherThread.handleOutOfRangeError(AbstractFetcherThread.scala:749)

On this call path, the leaderLocalLogStartOffset field in the message is the selected fetch start offset.

Dynamically setting follower.fetch.last.tiered.offset.enable=false bypassed this path and the follower recovered without a restart.

Code

TierStateMachine.java#L201-L238 (same on trunk):

long previousOffsetToLeaderLocalLogStartOffset = leaderLocalLogStartOffset - 1;
...
RemoteLogSegmentMetadata remoteLogSegmentMetadata = rlm.fetchRemoteLogSegmentMetadata(topicPartition, targetEpoch, previousOffsetToLeaderLocalLogStartOffset)
        .orElseThrow(() -> buildRemoteStorageException(...));

UnifiedLog.fetchEarliestPendingUploadOffset clamps its result to max(highestRemoteOffset + 1, logStartOffset), and AbstractFetcherThread.fetchEarliestPendingUploadOffset returns the local log start offset when nothing is uploaded and it equals the log start offset. So TierStateMachine can receive equal offsets during normal operation.

KIP-1023 describes this case as a normal local fetch: "it simply means that there are no valid log segments on the remote yet. Hence the ReplicaFetcher simply truncates its log and starts replicating all data the leader has locally."

Test gap

testLastTieredOffsetWithNonZeroLSOOnNewLeader and testLastTieredOffsetWithSlowUploadNoLocalDeletion in AbstractFetcherThreadTest cover equal positive start offsets, but both use MockTierStateMachine, which truncates directly to the selected offset and skips the metadata lookup. No test runs the real TierStateMachine in this case.

Proposed fix

In TierStateMachine.buildRemoteLogAuxState, when the fetch start offset equals the leader's log start offset, skip the earlier-epoch and remote metadata lookups, truncate fully to the leader's log start offset, and fetch from there. Keep the existing error when the remote range is not empty.

Related

  • KIP-1023 discussion: https://lists.apache.org/thread/ypwqnwyn7zn6xo781yjq4v99p44gv62h
  • Question on dev@: https://lists.apache.org/thread/94hv8gsn7hqsrsn2os7nh6qxz6lwp6y1

fields.description:
A follower hit by KAFKA-17249 claims the remote log range [logStartOffset, localLogStartOffset) without leader epoch entries for it, and nothing rebuilds them because its fetch offset is already inside the leader's local log.

When a replica becomes a follower and detects this, it should rebuild the remote log aux state from scratch. Resetting the fetch offset to logStartOffset is not enough: after a restart the follower's logStartOffset can lag the leader's, so the leader returns OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE and the fetcher resumes from the local log end offset, skipping the rebuild. Truncating the local log to logStartOffset first avoids that.

If the latest remote segment was uploaded by a leader with the same gap, the rebuilt cache has the gap again, so the rebuild should not be retried in a loop.

Discussion: https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23569#discussion_r4100224664

fields.description:
When the leader epoch cache of a leader does not cover its remote log range [logStartOffset, localLogStartOffset), which can happen to replicas hit by KAFKA-17249, the cleanup of unreferenced epochs in RemoteLogManager treats the remote segments of the missing epochs as unreferenced and deletes them. The remote tier is shared, so the data is lost for every replica.

RemoteLogManager should skip this deletion while the cache is incomplete. PR #23569 adds RemoteLogManager#isLeaderEpochCacheMissingRemoteEntries, which can be reused for the check.

Open questions:
- Such a leader also uploads its incomplete checkpoint with every new segment, so followers that later build their aux state from those segments inherit the gap. Should it skip copying segments too? The cost is that local segments cannot be deleted until they are copied.
- Skipping the deletion does not repair the leader, which still cannot serve the remote range. The missing entries could be filled from the checkpoint of the latest remote segment, if a healthy leader uploaded it, or rebuilt from the segment leader epochs in the remote log metadata. Both are larger changes.
- Filtering such replicas out of leader election would need the follower to report the state of its cache, which is a protocol change. With KAFKA-21191 , a broken follower cannot rejoin the ISR before it is rebuilt anyway, and when the broken replica is the only one in the ISR, filtering it out would make the partition unavailable.

Discussion: https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23569#discussion_r4100224664

fields.description:
SuppressionIntegrationTest takes about 290 seconds locally. 6 of its 14
cases take 42 to 46 seconds each, while the others take about 2 seconds.

Each test method uses a fixed application id, so the withHeaders=false and
withHeaders=true runs share one consumer group. The stream thread does not
leave the group on close, so the second run waits until the previous
member's session times out (45s).

shouldUseDefaultSerdes also reuses the "-shouldInheritSerdes" test id, so
it shares the group and topics with shouldInheritSerdes and its first run
waits as well.

The two shouldShutdownWhen... tests are not affected, because their members
send a LeaveGroup when the stream thread fails.

We can isolate each run with safeUniqueTestName(testInfo), as KAFKA-21133
did for FineGrainedAutoResetIntegrationTest.

JoinStoreIntegrationTest has the same issue: each of its two parameterized
tests reuses an application id across invocations, causing the second
invocation to wait for the previous member's session timeout. Include
both tests in the same fix by giving each invocation a unique application id.

fields.description:
KAFKA-20998 added \{{BalancedTaskAssignor}}, a one-to-one translation of the classic \{{HighAvailabilityTaskAssignor}} placement, not yet registered as a built-in. Its fix-up loop tests every pair of processes on each pass, so it costs Θ(P²) per pass even when nothing moves: up to 26x the sticky assignor's time in JMH (12.4 ms for 1000 single-member processes).

Plan:
# Index-based implementation and an O(P) early exit for passes that cannot move a task. Same assignment.
# Place active tasks with the Sainte-Laguë divisor method (next task to the process with the smallest (2n+1)/c), read from a precomputed period, instead of round-robin plus fix-up. Same placement for equal member counts; for unequal ones the same per-member balance and a more even spread of each subtopology. Separate PR, as it changes placement.
# Register \{{balanced}} in \{{GroupCoordinatorConfig.STREAMS_GROUP_BUILTIN_ASSIGNORS}} once KIP-1071 is amended from \{{highly_available}}.

Prototypes: 1 is 6-10x faster, 1+2 is 12-19x, about a quarter of the sticky assignor's time.
fields.summary: Speed up the balanced task assignor and register it as a built-in assignor

renderedFields.description:
KAFKA-20998 added BalancedTaskAssignor, a one-to-one translation of the classic HighAvailabilityTaskAssignor placement, not yet registered as a built-in. Its fix-up loop tests every pair of processes on each pass, so it costs Θ(P²) per pass even when nothing moves: up to 26x the sticky assignor's time in JMH (12.4 ms for 1000 single-member processes).

Plan:

  1. Index-based implementation and an O(P) early exit for passes that cannot move a task. Same assignment.
  2. Place active tasks with the Sainte-Laguë divisor method (next task to the process with the smallest (2n+1)/c), read from a precomputed period, instead of round-robin plus fix-up. Same placement for equal member counts; for unequal ones the same per-member balance and a more even spread of each subtopology. Separate PR, as it changes placement.
  3. Register balanced in GroupCoordinatorConfig.STREAMS_GROUP_BUILTIN_ASSIGNORS once KIP-1071 is amended from highly_available.

Prototypes: 1 is 6-10x faster, 1+2 is 12-19x, about a quarter of the sticky assignor's time.

ClientMetricsConfigs uses java.util.regex to compile the match patterns of client metrics subscriptions. We should switch to RE2/J, which is already used by the broker and guarantees linear time matching.

fields.description:
When CoordinatorExecutorImpl tasks are cancelled, they remain in the executor queue or the event processor queue. When the group coordinator is overloaded, these queues can grow large and retain data structures that are no longer needed.

One way we can allow the memory to be reclaimed by GC is to box the callbacks held by tasks and release them on cancellation.

fields.description:
The current los when an issue with the token leads to fail auth does not include anything to help identify the token, which makes it hard to correlate to the broker-side when a token is rejected.

Current client-side logging on token-related failure seems to be around principal only (debug level) here [https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/7aba83304c69e151597ecfb4e8a004079cdd1ec8/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/security/oauthbearer/internals/OAuthBearerRefreshingLogin.java#L106] 

and nothing is logged where I expect the token failure on the related incident would land on the client side [https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/7aba83304c69e151597ecfb4e8a004079cdd1ec8/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/security/oauthbearer/internals/OAuthBearerSaslClient.java#L100] 

This task is to review if logging could be improved (considering from the security pov, what would be helpful and acceptable to log)

This task is to review if logging could be improved (considering from the security pov, what would be helpful and acceptable to log)

fields.description:
ConsumerGroupMemberMetadataValue stores the full classic member metadata (session timeout and the protocol list with metadata bytes). Protocol metadata bytes are only used to fill the classic group on downgrade when no rebalance has happened since the group was reconstructed

The proposal is to keep only the protocol names (plus what is needed to rebuild the metadata, such as version and user data), or drop the metadata and force a rebalance on downgrade when a member's metadata is missing from the soft state

Compatibility is the main concern. Storing the full metadata means the broker never has to generate it. An old broker may not know how to handle the version the consumer uses. Any change must also stay compatible with records already written in the old format.

fields.description:
During log recovery, we discover offset overflow in a segment. If an overflow is detected, it stops the recovery and calls splitOverflowedSegment() to split the segment. However, since the segment hasn't been fully recovered, there could be untrimmed padding bytes in the segment if preallocation is enabled. This will cause an exception in splitOverflowedSegment() and fail log loading. The following call sequence shows how this can happen.

 
{code:java}
LogLoader.recoverLog()                                   LogLoader.java:456
  └─ retryOnOffsetOverflow(this::recoverLog)             :210  (outer) / :330 catch
       └─ recoverSegment(segment)                        :400
            └─ LogSegment.recover(...)                    LogSegment.java:482
                 for (RecordBatch batch : log.batches())  :490
                   batch.ensureValid()                    :491
                   ensureOffsetInRange(batch.lastOffset())  :492  ──► throws
                                                          LogSegmentOffsetOverflowException
  ── caught by retryOnOffsetOverflow ──                   LogLoader.java:330
       └─ LocalLog.splitOverflowedSegment(segment,...)    LocalLog.java:909
            while (position < sourceRecords.sizeInBytes())  :926  ◄── sizeInBytes() incl. padding
              sourceRecords.batchesFrom(position).iterator().next()  :927  ──► CorruptRecordException
              newSegment.appendFromFile(sourceRecords, position)     :930
                 appendChunkFromFile → records.batchesFrom(position).iterator()  LogSegment.java:294
{code}
 

Note that this issue likely won't happen in practice since the offset overflow case typically happens on existing rolled segment which has been trimmed.

fields.summary: ListOffset may return -1 when offset is available

comments.body: One way to fix this is to pass maxPosition for lastFetchableOffset into the search (as the fetch path already does for data reads) rather than relying on every caller to post-filter.

[~junrao] I'd like to pick this up if you're not planning to.

 

One thing to settle first: for MAX_TIMESTAMP, bounding the scan by position is not enough. The current UnifiedLog path first picks the segment with the globally greatest maxTimestampSoFar, then looks inside that segment. If that segment’s max timestamp is beyond the fetchable bound, we could return -1 even though the correct max timestamp exists in an earlier batch or segment.

 

So I think the fix needs to compute “max timestamp within the fetchable prefix,” which changes both segment selection and batch scanning. Also, since maxPosition is batch-granular and HW/LSO can fall mid-batch, I think the exclusive bound offset needs to be pushed down too, not just the file position, so we never return a record past the fetchable offset.

 

Does that match what you had in mind?

Also, the current FileRecords conflates:
 # the mutable, LEO-extent physical segment — {{{}append{}}}, {{{}truncateTo{}}}, {{{}readInto(pos){}}}, {{{}batchesFrom(pos){}}}, {{{}searchForTimestamp{}}}, used by storage internals/recovery/compaction/replication/raft; and
 # the immutable, offset-bounded read window produced by {{slice(pos, size)}} and handed to clients.

Claude suggested the following approach to clean it up.
h2. The design: split the mutable segment from the bounded view, with one chokepoint

Make the bound a type invariant instead of a field + convention.
 * {{LogFileRecords}} (internal physical segment) — owns the channel, {{{}start{}}}, {{{}end = size = LEO{}}}. Keeps the full/mutating/position API: {{{}append{}}}, {{{}truncateTo{}}}, {{{}readInto(buf,pos){}}}, {{{}batchesFrom(pos){}}}, {{{}slice{}}}. Visible only to storage internals, recovery, compaction, tiered upload, raft. Does not implement the client-facing {{Records}} interface, so it can never be passed where a {{Records}} is expected.
 * {{BoundedRecords}} (immutable, {{{}implements Records{}}}) — the window returned by {{{}slice(...){}}}. Exposes only whole-extent iteration/transfer ({{{}batches(){}}}, {{{}batchIterator(){}}}, {{{}writeTo{}}}, {{searchForTimestamp, }}{{{}sizeInBytes{}}}), with no arbitrary-position re-entry, no re-widening, no mutation. This is the only {{{}FileRecords{}}}-backed {{Records}} that flows into {{FetchDataInfo}} and responses (consumer, replication, share-fetch — all of which already go through {{{}read{}}}).
[~junrao]  please review [https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23780] when you get a chance.

fields.description:
h3. Problem

The Pull Request Linter rewrites PR descriptions with textwrap.fill(width=72), but its Markdown detection does not preserve valid indented lists or fenced code blocks. Editing the description to repair the formatting triggers the workflow again, so contributors repeatedly lose their formatting.

h3. Reproduction

On an open PR targeting trunk where the PR workflows can run:
# Put the following Markdown in the PR description. Each bullet starts with one space.
# Save the description and let Pull Request Reviewed and then Pull Request Linter complete.
# Inspect the description edit history and raw Markdown.

Input:
{noformat}
Example list:
 - first item
 - second item
{noformat}

Actual output:
{noformat}
Example list:  - first item  - second item
{noformat}

A second example demonstrates that a fenced code block is not a reliable workaround. Input:
{noformat}
```
first command

second command
third command

```
{noformat}

Actual output:
{noformat}
```
first command

second command third command

```
{noformat}

Both transformations were reproduced locally using the unmodified split_paragraphs function and formatting loop extracted from .github/scripts/pr-format.py at revision ef5c8dc99503176e0d7f5eb5068372d12f04d9df. Only the formatting logic was executed, without invoking the script's GitHub write path.

h3. Expected behavior

Linting or wrapping prose should preserve Markdown structure: list items and nesting must remain intact, and code block contents, indentation, line breaks and blank lines must remain unchanged. Subsequent linter runs should preserve these properties.

h3. Cause

* [pr-format.py|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/ef5c8dc99503176e0d7f5eb5068372d12f04d9df/.github/scripts/pr-format.py] checks line[0] for Markdown markers. A leading space means an indented list can be classified as prose, then joined and rewrapped.
* The Markdown flag resets at blank lines without tracking whether the parser is inside a fenced code block. Consequently, interior code paragraphs can be treated as prose. Even paragraphs recognized as Markdown have each line passed through textwrap.fill.
* The script writes the result back using gh pr edit --body-file.
* [pr-reviewed.yml|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/ef5c8dc99503176e0d7f5eb5068372d12f04d9df/.github/workflows/pr-reviewed.yml] runs on PR edits, and [pr-linter.yml|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/ef5c8dc99503176e0d7f5eb5068372d12f04d9df/.github/workflows/pr-linter.yml] invokes the formatter when that workflow succeeds.

h3. Related work and possible resolution

KAFKA-19013 introduced the intended 72-column preformatting behavior through [PR #19242|https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/19242]. This report concerns corruption of Markdown by that behavior.

Consider separating validation from description mutation, or limiting wrapping to prose using Markdown-aware parsing. Regression coverage should include indented and nested lists, fenced code blocks containing blank lines and long lines, and repeated formatting of the same input.

fields.environment: apache/kafka GitHub Actions PR workflows targeting trunk. Formatter verified at ef5c8dc99503176e0d7f5eb5068372d12f04d9df. This affects repository contribution tooling, not Kafka broker runtime.

  • The Markdown flag resets at blank lines without tracking whether the parser is inside a fenced code block. Consequently, interior code paragraphs can be treated as prose. Even paragraphs recognized as Markdown have each line passed through textwrap.fill.
  • The script writes the result back using gh pr edit --body-file.
  • pr-reviewed.yml runs on PR edits, and pr-linter.yml invokes the formatter when that workflow succeeds.

Related work and possible resolution

KAFKA-19013 introduced the intended 72-column preformatting behavior through PR #19242. This report concerns corruption of Markdown by that behavior.

Consider separating validation from description mutation, or limiting wrapping to prose using Markdown-aware parsing. Regression coverage should include indented and nested lists, fenced code blocks containing blank lines and long lines, and repeated formatting of the same input.

fields.description:
ReplaceField can read the wrong source field when transforming a Struct. A rename mapping remains in the global reverseRenames map even when its source field is excluded or absent from the input schema. If the rename target is an existing retained field, the schemaful path reads the excluded/missing source instead of that retained field.

Reproduction
1. Create an input Struct with INT32 fields a and b, with values a=1 and b=2.
2. Configure ReplaceField with exclude=a and renames=a:b.
3. Apply the transformation.

Expected: Struct{b=2}, with only the original b field retained.
Actual: Struct{b=1}; the excluded a value is copied into b.

A related case uses a schema containing only b, with renames=a:b. The transform should retain b, since a is absent. Instead, it attempts to read a and throws DataException. Incompatible source/target field types can also make the excluded-source case fail with DataException instead of silently changing the value.

Cause and proposed fix
makeUpdatedSchema filters input fields and applies forward renames, but applyWithSchema iterates output fields and uses a reverse map built from all configured renames. These operations disagree when a rename source did not contribute to the output schema. The focused fix is to iterate input schema fields, apply the same filter, and copy each retained value to its forward-renamed output field.

Verification
Reproduced on trunk commit 62f0fef0e81a8e24f6d174f9cf4b640620696e7c. With the proposed fix, all 301 connect-transforms module tests pass, including 19 ReplaceField tests; style checks pass. Released versions have not been tested.

Related work
KAFKA-10640 and https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/9493 concern broader recursive transformations. That PR is closed and unmerged and also proposed iterating input fields. This report is limited to incorrect source-field selection in the existing schemaful ReplaceField behavior.

fields.description:
*Description*

Server-side Streams rack-aware assignment configuration can accept tag keys longer than 20 characters, while the Kafka Streams client rejects such keys during {{StreamsConfig}} construction.

The inconsistency affects both configuration paths:
 * Broker default: {{group.streams.rack.aware.assignment.tags}}
 * Group override: {{streams.rack.aware.assignment.tags}}

For example, the server-side configuration accepts the following 22-character tag key:

 

{{streams.rack.aware.assignment.tags=availability_zone_name}}

However, a Streams client cannot supply the corresponding tag:
 * group.protocol=streams
 * client.tag.availability_zone_name=az-a

{{StreamsConfig}} throws a {{ConfigException}} because the tag key exceeds the client-side maximum length of 20 characters.

*Actual behavior*

The server accepts a rack-aware assignment tag key that the official Streams client cannot provide. Adding the corresponding client tag prevents the application from starting; omitting it leaves that tag unavailable to the assignor.

*Expected behavior*

Server-side rack-aware assignment configuration should be consistent with the tag keys supported by the Streams client. An unsupported key should be rejected when the configuration is supplied, rather than accepted and discovered later during client startup.

*Suggested fix*

Validate tag key lengths during broker bootstrap and Admin API group configuration changes. Reject keys longer than 20 characters with a {{ConfigException}} during bootstrap or the corresponding configuration error through the Admin API. (It would be better to consider length of value - 30)

Compatibility with previously stored configurations should be considered, particularly for configuration queries and metadata restoration.

fields.description:
*Description*

When a static member using {{group.protocol=streams}} restarts after removing its {{client.rack}} configuration, the coordinator retains the previous rack ID.

During static member replacement, the coordinator copies the previous member’s metadata and then treats {{RackId=null}} in the joining request as unchanged. Changing the rack ID to another value works, but removing it does not.

*Conditions*
 # Start a Streams application with {{group.instance.id}} and {{{}client.rack=rack-a{}}}.
 # Shut it down gracefully using the default close behavior.
 # Remove the {{client.rack}} configuration.
 # Restart with the same static instance ID before the session timeout expires.

*Expected behavior*

The coordinator should clear the rack ID to reflect the new client configuration. Since the rack has changed, the group epoch should increase and the assignment should be recomputed.

For regular heartbeats, {{RackId=null}} should continue to mean unchanged.

*Actual behavior*

The coordinator retains the previous rack ID. Group descriptions and custom assignors therefore receive stale rack information, and rack removal itself does not trigger assignment recomputation. If another metadata change triggers recomputation, the stale rack information is still used.
fields.summary: Removed client.rack configuration is not reflected when a Streams static member rejoins

renderedFields.description:
Description

When a static member using group.protocol=streams restarts after removing its client.rack configuration, the coordinator retains the previous rack ID.

During static member replacement, the coordinator copies the previous member’s metadata and then treats RackId=null in the joining request as unchanged. Changing the rack ID to another value works, but removing it does not.

Conditions

  1. Start a Streams application with group.instance.id and client.rack=rack-a.
  2. Shut it down gracefully using the default close behavior.
  3. Remove the client.rack configuration.
  4. Restart with the same static instance ID before the session timeout expires.

Expected behavior

The coordinator should clear the rack ID to reflect the new client configuration. Since the rack has changed, the group epoch should increase and the assignment should be recomputed.

For regular heartbeats, RackId=null should continue to mean unchanged.

Actual behavior

The coordinator retains the previous rack ID. Group descriptions and custom assignors therefore receive stale rack information, and rack removal itself does not trigger assignment recomputation. If another metadata change triggers recomputation, the stale rack information is still used.

fields.description:
Broker-side Streams custom assignor registration and group configuration handle surrounding whitespace differently.

{{GroupCoordinatorConfig.streamsGroupAssignors()}} uses the name returned by {{TaskAssignor.name()}} unchanged, while the group configuration {{streams.assignor.name}} applies {{trim()}} during STRING parsing.

For a custom assignor returning {{{}" regional "{}}}:
 * It can be used as the default assignor when registered first and no group override is set.
 * Explicitly setting {{streams.assignor.name=regional}} is rejected because it does not match the registered name.
 * Including the surrounding whitespace in the setting also fails because parsing removes it.
 * GROUP {{DescribeConfigs}} parses the default name as {{{}regional{}}}, so reapplying the reported value can also fail.
fields.summary: Reject leading and trailing whitespace in Streams custom assignor names

renderedFields.description:
Broker-side Streams custom assignor registration and group configuration handle surrounding whitespace differently.

GroupCoordinatorConfig.streamsGroupAssignors() uses the name returned by TaskAssignor.name() unchanged, while the group configuration streams.assignor.name applies trim() during STRING parsing.

For a custom assignor returning " regional ":

  • It can be used as the default assignor when registered first and no group override is set.
  • Explicitly setting streams.assignor.name=regional is rejected because it does not match the registered name.
  • Including the surrounding whitespace in the setting also fails because parsing removes it.
  • GROUP DescribeConfigs parses the default name as regional, so reapplying the reported value can also fail.

fields.description:
With the Streams protocol, the assignment tag list is determined by server-side configuration:
 * Broker default: {{group.streams.rack.aware.assignment.tags}}
 * Per-group override: {{streams.rack.aware.assignment.tags}}

The coordinator passes this list to the custom assignor. Clients provide their tag values through {{{}client.tag.*{}}}, while the client-side {{rack.aware.assignment.tags}} configuration is documented as ignored.

However, {{StreamsConfig}} still checks whether every tag in the client-side list is present. For example, even if the server uses {{{}zone{}}}, the following client configuration fails during construction because {{client.tag.cluster}} is missing:
 * group.protocol=streams
 * client.tag.zone=seoul
 * rack.aware.assignment.tags=cluster
fields.summary: Ignored client-side rack assignment tags can prevent Streams protocol clients from starting

renderedFields.description:
With the Streams protocol, the assignment tag list is determined by server-side configuration:

  • Broker default: group.streams.rack.aware.assignment.tags
  • Per-group override: streams.rack.aware.assignment.tags

The coordinator passes this list to the custom assignor. Clients provide their tag values through client.tag.*, while the client-side rack.aware.assignment.tags configuration is documented as ignored.

However, StreamsConfig still checks whether every tag in the client-side list is present. For example, even if the server uses zone, the following client configuration fails during construction because client.tag.cluster is missing:

  • group.protocol=streams
  • client.tag.zone=seoul
  • rack.aware.assignment.tags=cluster

fields.description:
Closing a Streams group dynamic member with {{REMAIN_IN_GROUP}} can leave the close future incomplete when the poll timer has expired.

{{StreamsMembershipManager.isLeavingGroup()}} returns {{false}} for dynamic members using {{{}REMAIN_IN_GROUP{}}}, even when their state is {{PREPARE_LEAVING}} or {{{}LEAVING{}}}. Consequently, {{StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestManager.poll()}} enters the poll timeout branch despite the member already leaving.

When the member is in {{{}LEAVING{}}}, {{onPollTimerExpired()}} attempts to transition it back to {{{}PREPARE_LEAVING{}}}, throwing:

 

{{IllegalStateException: Invalid state transition from LEAVING to PREPARE_LEAVING}}

This exception occurs before a heartbeat request is generated and prevents the normal path from skipping the leave heartbeat and completing the close future.

*Reproduction conditions*
 # Join a Streams group as a dynamic member without configuring {{{}group.instance.id{}}}.
 # Allow the application poll interval to exceed {{{}max.poll.interval.ms{}}}.
 # Before the heartbeat manager processes the poll timeout, process a close request with {{{}REMAIN_IN_GROUP{}}}, transitioning the member to {{{}LEAVING{}}}.
 # On the next heartbeat manager {{{}poll(){}}}, the invalid state transition exception occurs.

*Expected behavior*

Poll timeout handling should not initiate another leave operation while the member is already preparing to leave or leaving.

For a dynamic member closing with {{{}REMAIN_IN_GROUP{}}}, once the member reaches {{{}LEAVING{}}}, the client should skip the leave heartbeat, transition to {{{}UNSUBSCRIBED{}}}, and complete the close future normally.

While in {{{}PREPARE_LEAVING{}}}, regular heartbeats may continue until the pending callback completes.
fields.summary: Streams group dynamic member close can stall with REMAIN_IN_GROUP after poll timeout

renderedFields.description:
Closing a Streams group dynamic member with REMAIN_IN_GROUP can leave the close future incomplete when the poll timer has expired.

StreamsMembershipManager.isLeavingGroup() returns false for dynamic members using REMAIN_IN_GROUP, even when their state is PREPARE_LEAVING or LEAVING. Consequently, StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestManager.poll() enters the poll timeout branch despite the member already leaving.

When the member is in LEAVING, onPollTimerExpired() attempts to transition it back to PREPARE_LEAVING, throwing:

 

IllegalStateException: Invalid state transition from LEAVING to PREPARE_LEAVING

This exception occurs before a heartbeat request is generated and prevents the normal path from skipping the leave heartbeat and completing the close future.

Reproduction conditions

  1. Join a Streams group as a dynamic member without configuring group.instance.id.
  2. Allow the application poll interval to exceed max.poll.interval.ms.
  3. Before the heartbeat manager processes the poll timeout, process a close request with REMAIN_IN_GROUP, transitioning the member to LEAVING.
  4. On the next heartbeat manager poll(), the invalid state transition exception occurs.

Expected behavior

Poll timeout handling should not initiate another leave operation while the member is already preparing to leave or leaving.

For a dynamic member closing with REMAIN_IN_GROUP, once the member reaches LEAVING, the client should skip the leave heartbeat, transition to UNSUBSCRIBED, and complete the close future normally.

While in PREPARE_LEAVING, regular heartbeats may continue until the pending callback completes.

fields.description: KAFKA-21143 showcases a real use case: a broker that only validates incoming OAUTHBEARER tokens (inter-broker uses another mechanism) does not need a token of its own. Today the only way to get a tokenless login is to rely on the default OAuthBearerUnsecuredLoginCallbackHandler, which is documented as testing-only. The fix for KAFKA-21143 repairs that default path, but production users still deserve a dedicated, documented class that skips token retrieval.
fields.summary: Add tokenless OAuth login class

comments.body: Another option is to change the channel builder so that it skips login for listeners that do not need a token (non inter-broker listeners). However, that is a much bigger behavior change: custom login modules and callback handlers may rely on login being invoked

fields.description:
The classic protocol case of ColdStartStickinessIntegrationTest takes about
73 seconds locally, while the streams protocol case takes about 23 seconds.

After the first phase, the test closes both instances and waits for the
consumer group to become empty before the cold restart. With the classic
protocol, the stream threads do not leave the group on close, so the group
only becomes empty after both members' sessions time out (45s). The broker
logs show the members removed on heartbeat expiration about 44 seconds
after the close, and the restart begins right after that.

The streams protocol case is not affected, because dynamic members leave
the group on close by default.

We can set a shorter session timeout and heartbeat interval for the classic
protocol case, so the members expire shortly after the close. Leaving the
group on close does not work here, because the first instance's LeaveGroup
triggers a rebalance that can assign its tasks to the second instance
before it closes. Locally, a 6 second session timeout reduces the classic
case to about 34 seconds.

fields.summary: The cold snapshot timer should check pending updates instead of snapshot timestamps

renderedFields.description:
long coldSnapshottedPartitionsCount = shareStateMap.values().stream()
            .filter(shareGroupOffset -> shareGroupOffset.createTimestamp() - shareGroupOffset.writeTimestamp() != 0)
            .count();

        // If all share partitions are snapshotted, it means that
        // system is quiet and cold snapshotting will not help much.
        if (coldSnapshottedPartitionsCount == shareStateMap.size())

{             log.debug("All share snapshot records already cold snapshotted, skipping.");             return new CoordinatorResult<>(List.of(), null);         }

 

The early return treats "all partitions cold-snapshotted" as "system is quiet". But ShareUpdate does not touch createTimestamp or writeTimestamp (see merge()), so once every partition has been cold-snapshotted, the timer returns early on every run until some partition reaches the records threshold. Slow-traffic partitions are never flushed, which conflicts with the purpose of the timer.

fields.summary: AsyncKafkaConsumer passes null offsets to OffsetCommitCallback when an asynchronous commit fails

renderedFields.description:
When an asynchronous commit fails in AsyncKafkaConsumer with group.protocol=consumer, the user-provided OffsetCommitCallback receives null instead of the offsets associated with the request.

Both overloads are affected:

consumer.commitAsync(offsets, callback);
consumer.commitAsync(callback);

Successful commits pass the request offsets correctly.

Expected behavior

The callback should receive the offsets and metadata associated with the request, regardless of whether the commit succeeds or fails. The exception argument should indicate the failure and its cause.

This is consistent with the documentation for the offsets parameter of OffsetCommitCallback.onComplete() and the behavior of the Classic Consumer.

 

Actual behavior and impact

When an asynchronous commit fails, the callback is invoked as follows:

callback.onComplete(null, exception);

Applications cannot identify or log the offsets associated with the failed request using the callback argument. Error-handling code that accesses the offsets map may throw a NullPointerException.

consumer.commitAsync((offsets, exception) -> {
    if (exception != null)
{         offsets.forEach((partition, offset) ->             recordFailure(partition, offset, exception));     }
});

This issue concerns the information provided when reporting a failed commit. It does not imply that the issue itself causes commit failures or data loss.

 

Root cause

AsyncKafkaConsumer.commitAsync() forwards the committedOffsets value received by the commit future’s whenComplete handler directly to the user callback.

When the future completes exceptionally, committedOffsets` is `null`. The implementation does not fall back to the explicitly supplied request offsets. When offsets are omitted, the offsets calculated in the background are not separately retained for the failure callback either.

fields.description:
When transactional state stores (KIP-892) are enabled, we loosely bound our transaction buffers using the new {{statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes}}, which is checked in {{StreamThread#maybeCommit()}}.

However, {{TaskManager.commit()}} does not guarantee that it commits: if the thread is currently in the middle of a rebalance, *commits are skipped until it completes*. When this happens, processing continues without a commit until the rebalance has completed.

Long rebalances can therefore cause threads to exceed this limit by a large degree, potentially causing OOM errors (native memory, most likely).

I do not think this is a blocker for 4.4.0, because it only affects applications when transactional state stores have been explicitly enabled; and only under very specific circumstances.
fields.summary: Long rebalances can cause OOM errors with transactional state stores enabled

comments.body:
A simple solution would be to change the way our internal transaction buffers work.

Currently, our {{RocksDBTransactionBuffer}} works by maintaining two structures:
1. a {{WriteBatch}} of pending writes to apply to RocksDB; this is the native memory and is the primary reason {{statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes}} was introduced, because this memory is not counted against the block cache or write buffers.
2. a Java {{TreeMap}} that is used to serve reads of buffered writes. This essentially mirrors the contents of the {{WriteBatch}}, but in the JVM, and indexed.

The main reason the {{WriteBatch}} exists is to pay for the cost of writes during the {{put}}/{{delete}} operation; but this cost is very small ({{WriteBatch}} is very cheap).

Instead of holding this {{WriteBatch}} in-memory for the lifetime of the transaction, we can simply construct it during commit, by iterating the {{TreeMap}} and adding its contents to the {{WriteBatch}}.

This shifts more of the cost of writes from {{put}}/{{delete}} to {{commit}}; although I expect the total throughput to be similar.

Actually, there's one scenario where throughput might be improved: a low cardinality of keys with a high replacement/deletion rate. Since we would only replace them in the {{TreeMap}}, and then write only the most recent values in the {{WriteBatch}}, instead of replacing them in both.

Edit: actually, this would not really resolve the core problem, although it might help when there are many updates of the same key. Memory usage of the on-heap transaction buffer would still climb during a long rebalance, and peak native memory during commit would be essentially unchanged, because we still have to fill the {{WriteBatch}} with uncommitted records.

A more brute-force, but much simpler, approach would be for the StreamThread to halt processing once the {{statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes}} limit has been reached and not continue until the next commit succeeds.

As an aside: pausing processing under this circumstance could also be extended to a TimeoutException during commit: we would then wait for a successful commit before continuing processing, to prevent OOM issues.

I'm starting to lean towards *both* fixes: pausing processing until the next successful commit _and_ deferring the {{WriteBatch}} to commit-time.
