fields.summary: DefaultMessageFormatter should not pass the null literal to deserializers for null key/value

renderedFields.description:
private byte[] deserialize(ConsumerRecord<byte[], byte[]> consumerRecord, Optional<Deserializer<?>> deserializer, byte[] sourceBytes, String topic)

{         byte[] nonNullBytes = sourceBytes != null ? sourceBytes : nullLiteral;         return deserializer.map(value -> utfBytes(value.deserialize(topic, consumerRecord.headers(), nonNullBytes).toString())).orElse(nonNullBytes);     }

It looks like only the official StringDeserializer is safe from this logic. I guess we should just skip the deserializer and return nullLiteral instead.

fields.description:
Currently [StreamsGroupDescribeRequestTest|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/85387e94364bdf31c6acf06086210d85a9fb0711/core/src/test/scala/unit/kafka/server/StreamsGroupDescribeRequestTest.scala#L32] includes accidental JUnit 4 assert usages. Based on my findings:
 # Historically KAFKA-7339 had the JUnit 4 to JUnit 5 migration in scope.
 # KAFKA-19153 pulled in a new dependency [Mock OAuth2 Server|https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/no.nav.security/mock-oauth2-server/2.3.0] which in turn depends on JUnit 4
 # KAFKA-19754 probably only used the JUnit 4 asserts by accident since the test library is on the test classpath

As a fix I changed the asserts to the JUnit 5 equivalent and removed JUnit 4 from the test compile classpath so we can avoid similar accidents in the future.

Other things I considered:
 * JUnit 4 can't be excluded from [Mock OAuth2 Server|https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/no.nav.security/mock-oauth2-server/2.3.0] as it is a runtime dependency which results in NoClassDefFoundError
 * Tried updating [Mock OAuth2 Server|https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/no.nav.security/mock-oauth2-server/2.3.0] to latest version but it still pulls in JUnit 4
fields.summary: Remove accidental JUnit 4 usage

renderedFields.description:
Currently StreamsGroupDescribeRequestTest includes accidental JUnit 4 assert usages. Based on my findings:

  1. Historically KAFKA-7339 had the JUnit 4 to JUnit 5 migration in scope.
  2. KAFKA-19153 pulled in a new dependency Mock OAuth2 Server which in turn depends on JUnit 4
  3. KAFKA-19754 probably only used the JUnit 4 asserts by accident since the test library is on the test classpath

As a fix I changed the asserts to the JUnit 5 equivalent and removed JUnit 4 from the test compile classpath so we can avoid similar accidents in the future.

Other things I considered:

  • JUnit 4 can't be excluded from Mock OAuth2 Server as it is a runtime dependency which results in NoClassDefFoundError
  • Tried updating Mock OAuth2 Server to latest version but it still pulls in JUnit 4

 # KAFKA-19153 pulled in a new dependency [Mock OAuth2 Server|https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/no.nav.security/mock-oauth2-server/2.3.0] which in turn depends on JUnit 4
 # KAFKA-19754 probably only used the JUnit 4 asserts by accident since the test library is on the test classpath

As a fix I changed the asserts to the JUnit 5 equivalent and removed JUnit 4 from the test compile classpath so we can avoid similar accidents in the future.

 * JUnit 4 can't be excluded from [Mock OAuth2 Server|https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/no.nav.security/mock-oauth2-server/2.3.0] as it is a runtime dependency which results in NoClassDefFoundError
 * Tried updating [Mock OAuth2 Server|https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/no.nav.security/mock-oauth2-server/2.3.0] to latest version but it still pulls in JUnit 4

fields.description:
*Description*

{{MemberSubscriptionAndAssignmentImpl}} retains an {{Assignment}} that references the coordinator’s existing target assignment. Although {{Assignment}} wraps the outer map with {{{}Collections.unmodifiableMap(){}}}, the nested partition sets remain mutable.

If a custom assignor uses the input assignment as a working data structure and modifies a nested set, it also modifies the coordinator’s existing target assignment before returning the assignment result. 

 

KS also had similar issue https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20846 and it had been resolved.

 

*Actual Behavior*

A local reproduction of the Consumer path demonstrated the following:
 * The existing target assignment changes from \{0, 1} to \{1} during assignor execution.
 * {{TargetAssignmentBuilder}} considers the existing assignment and the returned result equal, so it does not generate a target assignment change record for the member.
 * The reverse index still retains the ownership information for partition 0.
 * Rolling back to the snapshot does not restore partition 0 in the nested set.

This can leave the coordinator’s in-memory state, reverse index, and logged state inconsistent.

*Expected Behavior*

The input assignment provided to the assignor should be immutable and isolated from coordinator state. Attempts to modify nested partition sets should be rejected without affecting the coordinator’s existing target assignment.

fields.description:
*Aqua Description :* jackson-databind binds a JSON string to a javax.xml.datatype.Duration or javax.xml.datatype.XMLGregorianCalendar field by passing the raw string verbatim to DatatypeFactory.newDuration(value) or newXMLGregorianCalendar(value) in CoreXMLDeserializers.Std._deserialize. These deserializers are registered by default with no opt-in, so a plain ObjectMapper or JsonMapper with no polymorphic typing and no special configuration reaches this path. The XML Schema lexical grammar permits numeric components of arbitrary length, which the JDK materializes through the native BigInteger(String) and BigDecimal(String) constructors, both quadratic in digit count. Because the digits sit inside a JSON string token rather than a JSON number token, jackson-core's StreamReadConstraints.maxNumberLength guard never applies; jackson's own NumberDeserializers call validateIntegerLength or validateFPLength before parsing a stringified number, but the XML datatype deserializer omits that pre-check. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore submit a single request of a few megabytes, such as a Duration value consisting of the letter P followed by several million digits and the letter Y, and force tens of seconds to several minutes of single-threaded CPU work; a handful of concurrent requests can saturate a server's worker threads. This affects com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 2.0.0 before 2.18.10, from 2.19.0 before 2.21.6, and from 2.22.0 before 2.22.2, and tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 3.0.0 before 3.1.6 and from 3.2.0 before 3.2.2. Users should upgrade to 2.18.10, 2.21.6, 2.22.2, 3.1.6, or 3.2.2.
*Vendor Statement :* null
*Vendor URL :* null
*NVD URL :* [https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-68497]
*Fix Version :* 2.18.10, 2.21.6, 2.22.2

 

*Aqua Description :* TypeDeserializerBase._findDeserializer() in FasterXML jackson-databind caches the resolved deserializer under the raw, attacker-supplied type ID. When name-based polymorphism is configured with a fallback, for example @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, defaultImpl = ...), every distinct unrecognized type ID resolves to the same fallback deserializer but is retained as its own key in the _deserializers map. That map has no configurable bound and lives for the lifetime of the type deserializer, so an attacker who can repeatedly supply fresh unknown type IDs causes monotonic memory retention across requests. The reporter observed 10,000 retained entries from 10,000 distinct unknown IDs, against a single entry for a control that repeated one unknown ID the same number of times, isolating attacker-controlled key cardinality from request volume. Exploitation requires an application that enables name-based polymorphism with a defaultImpl or equivalent fallback, accepts attacker-influenced type IDs, and reuses a long-lived ObjectMapper across requests. The fix stops caching fallback resolutions for unrecognized IDs and bounds both the number of cached entries and the length of a cacheable type ID.
*Vendor Statement :* null
*Vendor URL :* null
*NVD URL :* [https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-91776]
*Fix Version :* 2.18.11, 2.21.7, 2.22.3

fields.description:
Currently the max  number of consumers in a share consumer group is default to 200 and max to 1000.  In bigger platforms where batch processing along with slow consumer use cases limiting to just 1000 consumer is very restrictive.{*}{*}

One of the scenario is a batch processing of millions of records and having to parallel process 20-30k records in parallel using spring kafka concurrency feature would mean we would need at least 20-30k consumers in a consumer groups with around 1k pods. Current 1000 limit just let it have ~60pods.

Request this to be reevaluated and increase the number of consumers that a share group can have.

*group.share.max.size*
fields.summary: Increase the number of consumers in the share consumer group

comments.body:
[~prakhar1801] thanks for the report.

I'm not sure I follow why this workload needs 20–30k separate consumers. Share groups don't tie consumer count to partition count, so parallelism doesn't have to come from the number of consumer instances.

Because KafkaShareConsumer is not thread safe, did you try fewer consumers per pod and acking them from consumer thread once it is complete? and splitting the load across several share groups on the same topic.

Changing this limit group.share.max.size means changing several other dependent configs like group.share.max.share.sessions, rate limits, running bench marks and KIP etc.

(There is a KIP-1261 touching share group configs, but not this one in particular.)

Thanks for your response [~muralibasani] !

The problem with fewer consumer per pod is if I fetch say 5 messages per consumer and I have to ack them, I have to ack for all of them together which means if 4 messages takes 5secs and 1 message takes 1min all the other 4 threads are just waiting for the longest running one to complete. This impacts the overall throughput of the app.

re "and splitting the load across several share groups on the same topic"-- Can you explain bit more on this. My understanding is if I have more than one share group on a topic, consumers of the respective groups would get all the messages similar to how consumer groups work. So if I have one topic with 10 messages and 2 share groups with 1 consumer each, both share group consumers would get all the 10 messages.

I was discussing this with [~schofielaj] on the slack and was hoping to have a KIP to reevaluate this config for 4.5 or later.

I don't think KIP-1261 has really got off the ground yet. It does seem to me that we could accommodate increasing the maximum number of members in a share group, in particular now the way that rebalancing in the group coordinator has got more sophisticated.
[~schofielaj] I would be happy to write the KIP, if you're fine with it. However need your inputs on the coordinator side and benchmarks.

[^assignor-gc-G1.json]  [^assignor-gc-Parallel.json]  [^assignor-sweep-pretouch.json]  [^hashmap-isolated.json]  [^MapBench.java]  [^notes.txt]  [^working-set.json]  [^WorkingSetBench.java] [~muralibasani] [~schofielaj] Following up on the request for benchmarks, I'd be happy to contribute measurements to support the KIP.

As a first step, I measured the share group assignor beyond 1,000 members with the existing ShareGroupAssignorBenchmark, overriding its parameters (trunk f908227639, SimpleAssignor, full assignment, homogeneous subscription, 10 topics with 10 partitions each; Apple M2 Max, JDK 17, fixed 8 GiB heap with AlwaysPreTouch, 5 forks):

||Members||Assignment (ms/op)||Time per member (ns)||Allocation per member (bytes)||
|10,000|1.47|147|907|
|30,000|5.42|181|920|
|60,000|12.59|210|920|
|100,000|25.54|255|931|

Allocated bytes per member stay roughly constant, while the time per member increases. I haven't isolated the cause of that increase. Measurement details and tentative observations are in the attached notes; raw results and synthetic benchmark sources are attached separately. This covers only the assignor, so it doesn't establish an acceptable limit or the coordinator and broker capacity.

Would coordinator processing and assignment-record volume, or broker share-session capacity, be the more useful next focus for the KIP?

As a first step, I measured the share group assignor beyond 1,000 members with the existing ShareGroupAssignorBenchmark, overriding its parameters (trunk f908227639, SimpleAssignor, full assignment, homogeneous subscription, 10 topics with 10 partitions each; Apple M2 Max, JDK 17, fixed 8 GiB heap with AlwaysPreTouch, 5 forks):

Members Assignment (ms/op) Time per member (ns) Allocation per member (bytes)
10,000 1.47 147 907
30,000 5.42 181 920
60,000 12.59 210 920
100,000 25.54 255 931

Allocated bytes per member stay roughly constant, while the time per member increases. I haven't isolated the cause of that increase. Measurement details and tentative observations are in the attached notes; raw results and synthetic benchmark sources are attached separately. This covers only the assignor, so it doesn't establish an acceptable limit or the coordinator and broker capacity.

fields.summary: Producer: concurrent first sends can wait an extra retry.backoff.ms for a redundant metadata refresh

comments.body: A fix is available for review in https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23753.

renderedFields.description:
Issue

We run a producer with metadata.max.idle.ms at its default (5 min) and retry.backoff.ms=750. When a topic has been idle longer than metadata.max.idle.ms and several threads call send() at about the same time, some of them occasionally block for roughly 900 ms inside send(). That is about one retry.backoff.ms, even though the brokers are healthy and the first metadata response comes back in a couple of milliseconds. In our case two threads that called send() within ~2 ms of each other were both stuck for ~897 ms and were released together.

Description

  1. In KafkaProducer.waitOnMetadata() the thread first takes a snapshot with metadata.fetch(), then calls metadata.requestUpdateForTopic(topic). These are two separate lock acquisitions. If the sender thread applies the first metadata response in between: ProducerMetadata.update() removes the topic from newTopics, bumps updateVersion (V -> V+1), and sets lastRefreshMs = now.
  2. The waiting thread still has the old snapshot (no partitions for the topic), so it does not take the fast path.
  3. It calls requestUpdateForTopic(topic). The topic is no longer in newTopics, so this goes to requestUpdate(false). That only sets needFullUpdate and returns V+1.
  4. awaitUpdate(V+1) now needs a second metadata response, but a new refresh is not allowed until lastRefreshMs + retry.backoff.ms (with jitter), so the thread sits there for ~0.6-0.9 s at 750 ms.

The data the thread needs is already in the metadata at step 2, so the wait is redundant. When the second response arrives, all the threads that hit this window wake up together.
If requestUpdateForTopic() happens before the response is applied, the topic is still in newTopics, requestUpdateForNewTopics() is used (no backoff), and the thread is released by the first response. So only the interleaving decides.

Reproduction

The race is also reproducible with a real KafkaProducer.

Test setup: one producer, metadata.max.idle.ms=5000, metadata.max.age.ms=1000, retry.backoff.ms=750, brokers ~35 ms away. Every cycle: wait until the topic is evicted from the producer metadata, send from one "trigger" thread, then send from 100 other threads at randomized instants spread over a ~20 ms window around the time the first metadata response is expected. Plain simultaneous start does not hit it, because all threads then arrive before the first response is applied; the arrivals have to be spread around the moment the response is applied.

Since the window is the time between fetch() and requestUpdateForTopic(), the example below shows the same.

public class MetadataRaceProbe {
    public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
        String topic = "probe";
        int probes = 100;
        long spreadMs = 20, pauseMs = 7_000, stallMs = 400;
        long estimateMs = 40;                // initial guess of the metadata round trip
 
        Properties p = new Properties();
        p.put("bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092");
        p.put("key.serializer", ByteArraySerializer.class.getName());
        p.put("value.serializer", ByteArraySerializer.class.getName());
        p.put("metadata.max.idle.ms", "5000");     // minimum Kafka allows
        p.put("metadata.max.age.ms", "1000");      // refresh often so eviction happens inside the pause
        p.put("retry.backoff.ms", "750");
        // + security settings if needed
 
        KafkaProducer<byte[], byte[]> producer = new KafkaProducer<>(p);
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(probes + 1);
        byte[] payload = "x".getBytes();
 
        for (int cycle = 0; cycle < 85; cycle++) {
            long t0 = System.nanoTime() + 100_000_000L;          // common start, 100 ms ahead
            long est = estimateMs * 1_000_000L, spread = spreadMs * 1_000_000L;
 
            Future<Long> trigger = pool.submit(timedSend(producer, topic, payload, t0));
            List<Future<Long>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
            long slot = spread / probes;
            for (int i = 0; i < probes; i++) {
                long offset = -spread / 2 + i * slot + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(slot);
                fs.add(pool.submit(timedSend(producer, topic, payload, t0 + Math.max(0, est + offset))));
            }
 
            long triggerMs = trigger.get();
            List<Long> stalls = new ArrayList<>();
            for (Future<Long> f : fs) { long ms = f.get(); if (ms >= stallMs) stalls.add(ms); }
 
            boolean evicted = triggerMs >= 5;            // trigger paid a metadata round trip
            System.out.printf("cycle=%d evicted=%b trigger=%dms stalledProbes=%d %s%n",
                    cycle, evicted, triggerMs, stalls.size(), stalls);
 
            if (cycle > 0 && triggerMs >= 5 && triggerMs < stallMs)
                estimateMs = (estimateMs * 3 + triggerMs) / 4;   // follow the real RTT
            Thread.sleep(pauseMs);                           // > idle + age, so the topic gets evicted
        }
        pool.shutdownNow();
        producer.close();
    }

    static Callable<Long> timedSend(KafkaProducer<byte[], byte[]> producer, String topic, byte[] payload, long targetNanos) {
        return () -> {
            waitUntil(targetNanos);
            long t = System.nanoTime();
            Future<RecordMetadata> ack = producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(topic, payload));
            long sendMs = TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(System.nanoTime() - t);
            ack.get();
            return sendMs;
        };
    }


    static void waitUntil(long target) {
        long left;
        while ((left = target - System.nanoTime()) > 0) {
            if (left > 200_000) LockSupport.parkNanos(left - 150_000);
            else Thread.onSpinWait();
        }
    }
}

Expected behavior

A thread whose snapshot is older than an already-applied metadata update should not schedule a new refresh. It should just re-read the metadata, find the topic, and carry on.

comments.body: A fix is available for review in https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23753.

Updated steps to reproduce - previous version had less concurrency and was harder t reproduce with short local RTT inside localhost

 

public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
    String topic = "probe";
    ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
    int probes = 5000;
    long pauseMs = 8_000, stallMs = 400;
    long estimateMs = 40;                // initial guess of the metadata round trip

    Properties p = new Properties();
    p.put("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092");
    p.put("key.serializer", ByteArraySerializer.class.getName());
    p.put("value.serializer", ByteArraySerializer.class.getName());
    p.put("metadata.max.idle.ms", "5000");     // minimum Kafka allows
    p.put("metadata.max.age.ms", "1000");      // refresh often so eviction happens inside the pause
    p.put("retry.backoff.ms", "750");
    // + security settings if needed

    KafkaProducer<byte[], byte[]> producer = new KafkaProducer<>(p);
    byte[] payload = "x".getBytes();

    for (int cycle = 0; cycle < 11; cycle++) {
        CountDownLatch startingGun = new CountDownLatch(1);

        List<Future<Long>> fs = new ArrayList<>();

        Future<Long> trigger = pool.submit(() -> {
            startingGun.await(); // Wait for the signal
            long t = System.nanoTime();
            producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(topic, payload)).get();
            return TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(System.nanoTime() - t);
        });

        for (int i = 0; i < probes; i++) {
            fs.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                startingGun.await();
                long t = System.nanoTime();
                producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(topic, payload)).get();
                return TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(System.nanoTime() - t);
            }));
        }

        startingGun.countDown();

        long triggerMs = trigger.get();
        List<Long> stalls = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Future<Long> f : fs) {
            long ms = f.get();
            if (ms >= stallMs) stalls.add(ms);
        }

        boolean evicted = triggerMs >= 5;
        System.out.printf("cycle=%d evicted=%b trigger=%dms stalledProbes=%d %s%n",
                cycle, evicted, triggerMs, stalls.size(), stalls);

        if (cycle > 0 && triggerMs >= 5 && triggerMs < stallMs)
            estimateMs = (estimateMs * 3 + triggerMs) / 4;
        Thread.sleep(pauseMs);
    }
    pool.shutdownNow();
    producer.close();
}

fields.summary: Server-side consumer regex subscriptions do not honor `exclude.internal.topics`

comments.body:
[~lianetm] Hi!

My understanding is that *{{SubscriptionPattern}}* was introduced as part of KIP-848.
Could you please clarify whether it is intended to honor the client-side *{{exclude.internal.topics}}* configuration?

If it is, it seems that the client would need to include this setting in the API request sent to the server.
I would appreciate your thoughts on this! :)

Hey [~chickenchickenlove] , interesting case, thanks for reporting!

Agree with the gap, on the client we're ignoring that config when the assignment comes from re2j (not intentional, just a miss), but this is bigger than that, the assignment path for the regex needs to consider it and fix at the source (with client side drop only the topic would remain assigned to this member from the GC pov, wrong).

There is some ongoing work around the broker-side regex that may include this (they linked their jira). I would say we follow that broker-side work first, and then we can assess if there is anything else we may need to do. Makes sense?

Thanks, good catch!

[~lianetm] 

Thanks for the detailed explanation!

That makes sense. I agree that the issue should be addressed on the broker side first, since a client-side fix alone could leave the assignment inconsistent with the group coordinator's view. I'll keep an eye on the broker-side work and Happy to help with any follow-up work if needed.

[~chickenchickenlove] As a first step, we could filter out the internal topics when the regex is resolved on the server side. I think that it is a better default behavior than the current implementation. We could backport this fix to previous versions too. Then, we can discuss whether we want to bring the config back when we discuss the design of KAFKA-21254. Would you be interested by doing this first step?

David, we also need to consider the compatibility implications of the change. Is there a reasonable case where someone might be relying on the accidental behavior? The safest option where we have the more intuitive default is to have a way to disable the new behavior.

[~dajac] 

Yes, I'd be happy to work on this!

Considering Ismael's feedback, should we also consider introducing a dynamic broker configuration? For example, we could add a server-side config such as {{{}exclude.internal.topics{}}}, defaulting to {{{}true{}}}, and allow users to set it to {{false}} via the Dynamic Config API. (However, this might require us to consider another deprecation sequence when we refactor this as part of KAFKA-21254.)

If that adds too much complexity, I could start with a simpler implementation that always filters out internal topics without introducing a new configuration.

renderedFields.description:
Description

When using SubscriptionPattern with group.protocol=consumer, server-side regex subscriptions do not honor exclude.internal.topics=true. The same issue occurs when the configuration is omitted, since its default value is true.

Java Pattern subscriptions correctly exclude internal topics under the same consumer protocol. This creates inconsistent configuration behavior between the two regex subscription APIs.

 

Conditions

  • group.protocol=consumer
  • exclude.internal.topics=true, or the configuration is omitted
  • A regex that also matches internal topic names, such as SubscriptionPattern(".*")
  • An internal topic, such as __consumer_offsets, exists in the coordinator metadata
  • The consumer has the required permissions to describe and read the topic

Example configuration and subscription:

props.put("group.protocol", "consumer");
props.put("exclude.internal.topics", "true");

consumer.subscribe(new SubscriptionPattern(".*"));

 

Expected Behavior

Internal topics should be excluded from the subscription and assignment even when they match the regex.

With exclude.internal.topics=false, matching internal topics should remain eligible for subscription. Explicit subscriptions by topic name should also preserve the existing contract: internal topics may be explicitly subscribed to even when the setting is true.

 

Observed Behavior and Cause

For Java Pattern subscriptions, the client evaluates the regex against metadata that excludes internal topics and sends the matching topic names in the heartbeat's SubscribedTopicNames field.

For SubscriptionPattern subscriptions, the client sends the regex string in SubscribedTopicRegex. The current heartbeat schema has no field for conveying the internal-topic exclusion setting, and TopicRegexResolver evaluates the regex against all topic names without excluding internal topics.

Additionally, ConsumerMetadata.retainTopic(...) retains metadata for topic IDs assigned through server-side regex subscriptions using the following condition:

return retainTopic(topicName, isInternal, nowMs)
    || subscription.isAssignedFromRe2j(topicId);

Consequently, metadata is retained for a topic ID assigned by the server even when the internal-topic exclusion check returns false.

fields.description:
I was testing compacted topics and noticed that there is no official tool to write a tombstone for a specific record. The console producer can produce null values (KIP-810), but there is no way to type a binary key, so records with serialized keys (long, Avro, Protobuf, etc.) cannot be deleted from the command line.

Of course, we can leverage AI to generate 1000 tools immediately, but “this tool” can be addressed by supporting hex 🙂

Also, hex is the baseline for all types of records. It is line-safe, so the output can be piped through grep, awk, and other console tools, and it can be fed back into the console producer to reproduce the exact same bytes.

fields.summary: AsyncKafkaConsumer may auto-commit offsets for records not yet returned to the application

renderedFields.description:
AsyncKafkaConsumer may include offsets for records that have not yet been returned to application code in a periodic auto-commit. If the commit succeeds and the application terminates before processing those records, they may be skipped after restart, violating at-least-once processing semantics.

This can happen even when the application processes every record returned by one poll() before calling poll() again:

while (running) {
    ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(timeout);

    for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> record : records) {
        process(record);
    }
}

AsyncKafkaConsumer.poll() submits an AsyncPollEvent to the background thread. When buffered records are available and the required conditions are satisfied, the application thread can collect those records before the event has finished processing.

Collecting records advances SubscriptionState.position to the next offset to read. This update occurs before poll() returns to the application and does not indicate that application code has finished processing the records.

However, the background thread calls subscriptions.allConsumed() when processing the AsyncPollEvent to determine which offsets to auto-commit. It can therefore use a position that the application thread has already advanced within the current poll() call.

Consider the following state for a single partition:

  • enable.auto.commit=true, and the auto-commit interval has elapsed.
  • The application has finished processing all records through offset 99.
  • Both the committed offset stored on the broker and the current consumer position are 100.
  • Records at offsets 100 and 101 are available in the fetch buffer.

The following execution sequence is possible:

  1. Application code calls consumer.poll().All records from the previous poll() have already been processed. The records at offsets 100 and 101 have not yet been delivered to application code.
  2. The application thread submits an AsyncPollEvent.Before the background thread processes this event, the application thread can proceed to collect buffered records.
  3. The application thread collects the records at offsets 100 and 101 and advances the position to 102.At this point, poll() may not have returned yet. The internal consumer position is 102, but application code may still be waiting to receive the two records.
  4. The background thread processes the delayed AsyncPollEvent. Since the auto-commit interval has elapsed, it calls allConsumed(). This method reads the current shared state and returns offset 102, which is then included in the auto-commit request.
  5. The background thread sends the commit request, and the broker stores offset 102. This can complete while execution of the application thread is delayed. Consequently, a resume position that skips these records can be stored before they have even been returned to the application.
  6. The application terminates before poll() returns. The records at offsets 100 and 101 have never been delivered to application code, so process(record) has not been called for either record. However, offset 102 has already been committed on the broker.
  7. The same consumer group resumes consumption from the committed offset. Consumption starts at offset 102. The records at offsets 100 and 101 are skipped without ever having been processed by application code.

In this example, the safe offset to commit when the current poll() begins is 100. Reading the shared position when the event is processed instead produces offset 102, which includes the records collected by the current poll().

The issue is a race between the position update inside poll() and the background thread’s determination of the offsets to auto-commit. It does not depend on how quickly application code processes returned records: the commit can advance before those records are delivered to the application.

 * Records at offsets 100 and 101 are available in the fetch buffer.

The following execution sequence is possible:
 # *Application code calls {{{}consumer.poll(){}}}.*

All records from the previous {{poll()}} have already been processed. The records at offsets 100 and 101 have not yet been delivered to application code.

 # *The application thread submits an {{{}AsyncPollEvent{}}}.*

Before the background thread processes this event, the application thread can proceed to collect buffered records.

 # *The application thread collects the records at offsets 100 and 101 and advances the position to 102.*

At this point, {{poll()}} may not have returned yet. The internal consumer position is 102, but application code may still be waiting to receive the two records.

 # *The background thread processes the delayed {{{}AsyncPollEvent{}}}.*

Since the auto-commit interval has elapsed, it calls {{{}allConsumed(){}}}. This method reads the current shared state and returns offset 102, which is then included in the auto-commit request.

 # *The background thread sends the commit request, and the broker stores offset 102.*

This can complete while execution of the application thread is delayed. Consequently, a resume position that skips these records can be stored before they have even been returned to the application.

 # *The application terminates before {{poll()}} returns.*

The records at offsets 100 and 101 have never been delivered to application code, so {{process(record)}} has not been called for either record. However, offset 102 has already been committed on the broker.

 # *The same consumer group resumes consumption from the committed offset.*

Consumption starts at offset 102. The records at offsets 100 and 101 are skipped without ever having been processed by application code.

In this example, the safe offset to commit when the current {{poll()}} begins is 100. Reading the shared position when the event is processed instead produces offset 102, which includes the records collected by the current {{{}poll(){}}}.

The issue is a race between the position update inside {{poll()}} and the background thread’s determination of the offsets to auto-commit. It does not depend on how quickly application code processes returned records: the commit can advance before those records are delivered to the application.

{{AsyncKafkaConsumer}} may include offsets for records that have not yet been returned to application code in a periodic auto-commit. If the commit succeeds and the application terminates before processing those records, they may be skipped after restart, violating at-least-once processing semantics.

This can happen even when the application processes every record returned by one {{poll()}} before calling {{poll()}} again:
{code:java}
while (running) {
    ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(timeout);

    for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> record : records) {
        process(record);
    }
} {code}
{{AsyncKafkaConsumer.poll()}} submits an {{AsyncPollEvent}} to the background thread. When buffered records are available and the required conditions are satisfied, the application thread can collect those records before the event has finished processing.

Collecting records advances {{SubscriptionState.position}} to the next offset to read. This update occurs before {{poll()}} returns to the application and does not indicate that application code has finished processing the records.

However, the background thread calls {{subscriptions.allConsumed()}} when processing the {{AsyncPollEvent}} to determine which offsets to auto-commit. It can therefore use a position that the application thread has already advanced within the current {{poll()}} call.

 * {{{}enable.auto.commit=true{}}}, and the auto-commit interval has elapsed.

 * Both the committed offset stored on the broker and the current consumer position are 100.

fields.description:
When using the Java {{AsyncKafkaConsumer}} with {{group.protocol=consumer}} and {{{}enable.auto.commit=true{}}}, a pre-rebalance auto-commit retry may commit an offset beyond records that the application has not yet processed.

When CommitRequestManager.autoCommitSyncBeforeRebalanceWithRetries() receives a retriable error, it calls {{subscriptions.allConsumed()}} again and replaces the existing request’s offset map. These offsets reflect consumer positions advanced while collecting records for {{{}poll(){}}}, rather than the application’s processing progress.

During a rebalance, record collection is blocked for partitions pending revocation, but records can still be returned from retained partitions. Although the revocation and assignment sequence waits for the auto-commit to complete, the application thread does not wait for the entire commit retry sequence. Consequently, the following sequence is possible:
 # After the application finishes processing records through offset 99 in partition P, a pre-rebalance auto-commit starts with offset 100.
 # While the initial commit request is pending, {{poll()}} returns records 100–149 from retained partition P. The internal position advances to 150, and the application starts processing the batch.
 # The initial commit request fails with a retriable error.
 # The retry logic reads the current position again, changing the offset to commit from 100 to 150.
 # If offset 150 is committed and the process exits before processing the entire batch, the restarted consumer may resume from 150 and skip the remaining unprocessed records.

This can occur even when a single application thread follows the sequence {{{}poll → process all returned records → next poll{}}}. It does not require the periodic auto-commit interval to expire.

An auto-commit retry should not commit beyond the application’s processing progress. However, this retry path can include positions advanced by records returned after the initial request was created. This may cause records to remain unprocessed by the consumer group after a failure.
fields.summary: Pre-rebalance auto-commit retries may commit offsets beyond unprocessed records

renderedFields.description:
When using the Java AsyncKafkaConsumer with group.protocol=consumer and enable.auto.commit=true, a pre-rebalance auto-commit retry may commit an offset beyond records that the application has not yet processed.

When CommitRequestManager.autoCommitSyncBeforeRebalanceWithRetries() receives a retriable error, it calls subscriptions.allConsumed() again and replaces the existing request’s offset map. These offsets reflect consumer positions advanced while collecting records for poll(), rather than the application’s processing progress.

During a rebalance, record collection is blocked for partitions pending revocation, but records can still be returned from retained partitions. Although the revocation and assignment sequence waits for the auto-commit to complete, the application thread does not wait for the entire commit retry sequence. Consequently, the following sequence is possible:

  1. After the application finishes processing records through offset 99 in partition P, a pre-rebalance auto-commit starts with offset 100.
  2. While the initial commit request is pending, poll() returns records 100–149 from retained partition P. The internal position advances to 150, and the application starts processing the batch.
  3. The initial commit request fails with a retriable error.
  4. The retry logic reads the current position again, changing the offset to commit from 100 to 150.
  5. If offset 150 is committed and the process exits before processing the entire batch, the restarted consumer may resume from 150 and skip the remaining unprocessed records.

This can occur even when a single application thread follows the sequence poll → process all returned records → next poll. It does not require the periodic auto-commit interval to expire.

An auto-commit retry should not commit beyond the application’s processing progress. However, this retry path can include positions advanced by records returned after the initial request was created. This may cause records to remain unprocessed by the consumer group after a failure.

fields.description:
In Zookeeper, there is a Hierarchical Quorums mechanism to allow to set some nodes to have groups/weights to have higher possibility to be elected as the leader.

[https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/r3.9.4/zookeeperInternals.html#sc_quorum]

[https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/r3.9.4/zookeeperHierarchicalQuorums.html]

 

The use case is that when there are 3 data center: 

Datacenter A: 2 controllers
Datacenter B: 2 controllers
Datacenter C: 1 controller

 

The data center C has a more unstable network and constraint resource. We don't want it to become the active leader to increase the overhead for it.

 

The expected behavior would be:

1. Controllers in Datacenters A and B are preferred during normal elections.

2. The controller in Datacenter C remains a full voter and continues contributing to quorum.

3. The controller in Datacenter C can still become Active Controller when required for availability.

4. Under normal conditions, Datacenter C should have a lower probability or priority of becoming Active Controller than controllers in Datacenters A and B.
fields.summary: KRaft Controller Election Preference Mechanism

comments.body: Hello [~showuon], if you’re not currently working on this, I’d be interested in picking it up. Thanks!

[~showuon] I have a few questions:
 * *What is the actual goal?* Is it latency (keep the leader in a particular DC), durability (every commit must reach C), or a C-as-witness setup? Notethat with 2-2-1, losing any single DC already leaves at least 3 voters, so the current design already survives one DC outage. Why AB is a problem needs to be stated.
 * *Is leader preference enough?* If so, it's a small, low-risk change built on the existing PreferredCandidates and backoff mechanism.
 * {*}If quorum rules really have to change{*}, how should it interact with KIP-853 voter add and remove? Should groups and weights be stored in the voter set inside the log?

> *What is the actual goal?* Is it latency (keep the leader in a particular DC), durability (every commit must reach C), or a C-as-witness setup? Notethat with 2-2-1, losing any single DC already leaves at least 3 voters, so the current design already survives one DC outage. Why AB is a problem needs to be stated.

 

It's reliability I would say. In our example, the DC c is a resource constraint node, which we don't want it to be elected as the leader. I've updated the expected behavior in the description above.

 

> *Is leader preference enough?* If so, it's a small, low-risk change built on the existing PreferredCandidates and backoff mechanism.

 

I think so. But not sure if there are other requests from the community to make it more flexible. 

 

> {*}If quorum rules really have to change{*}, how should it interact with KIP-853 voter add and remove? Should groups and weights be stored in the voter set inside the log?

 

Yes, in KIP-853, the source of truth for the voter info is the metadata log, not the kafka proerties file anymore. So I'd also expect the weight store in the metadata log. Of course, it needs more discussion in the community.

 

Thank you for picking it up.

fields.summary: kafka-streams-groups.sh --describe --topology: global store sub-topology label can collide with a real subtopology id

renderedFields.description:
Problem

TopologyDescriptionFormatter (tools/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/tools/streams/TopologyDescriptionFormatter.java) labels global stores starting at topology.subtopologies().size():
 
 {{int globalStoreId = topology.subtopologies().size();

for (final GlobalStore globalStore : topology.globalStores())

{ appendGlobalStore(sb, globalStore, globalStoreId++);}

}}
This assumes regular subtopologies are numbered 0..N-1. In Kafka Streams, global stores and subtopologies share one node-group id counter (InternalTopologyBuilder), so if the app defines its global store/table first, the global store gets id 0 and regular subtopologies get 1..N.

Example

Global store defined first, then two regular subtopologies (real ids 1, 2). CLI output:
 
 Sub-topology: 1Sub-topology: 2Sub-topology: 2 for global store (will not generate tasks) <- collides with real sub-topology 2
Stock Streams TopologyDescription.toString() would label the global store 0.

Impact

Cosmetic, CLI display only (KIP-1331 --describe --topology). Stored/pushed topology data and the CRD are unaffected. Not a release blocker; can confuse operators reading the output.

val proposedAssignmentForNewPartitions = replicaAssignment.getOrElse {
      val startIndex = math.max(0, allBrokers.indexWhere(_.id >= existingAssignmentPartition0.head))
      CoreUtils.replicaToBrokerAssignmentAsScala(AdminUtils.assignReplicasToBrokers(allBrokers.asJava, partitionsToAdd, existingAssignmentPartition0.size,
        startIndex, existingAssignment.size))
    }

The zk broker picks partition 0’s replicas for the newly created partitions.

        Iterator<PartitionRegistration> iterator = topicInfo.parts.values().iterator();
        if (!iterator.hasNext()) {
            throw new UnknownServerException("Invalid state: topic " + topic.name() +
                " appears to have no partitions.");
        }
        PartitionRegistration partitionInfo = iterator.next();
        if (partitionInfo.replicas.length > Short.MAX_VALUE) {
            throw new UnknownServerException("Invalid replication factor " +
                partitionInfo.replicas.length + ": expected a number equal to less than " +
                Short.MAX_VALUE);
        }
        short replicationFactor = (short) partitionInfo.replicas.length;

By contrast, the kraft broker picks the "first" partition, but the "first" depends on the hash slot layout. Hence, it is unpredictable to users

It can be fixed simply by replacing the `.next` to `parts.get(0)`

fields.description:
With exactly-once enabled, a commitTransaction() call that times out (max.block.ms) leaves the producer with a pending commit that was never acknowledged. Any later abortTransaction() on that producer throws IllegalStateException: "Cannot attempt operation abortTransaction because the previous call to commitTransaction timed out and must be retried".

RecordCollectorImpl.closeDirty() calls streamsProducer.abortTransaction() before close(). StreamsProducer.abortTransaction() doesn't catch IllegalStateException, so the exception escapes closeDirty(). As a result, close() is skipped and the collector's offsets map is not cleared. StreamTask.close() swallows the exception in TaskManager.executeAndMaybeSwallow(), which logs only at DEBUG and doesn't include the exception.

A task revived after the dirty close reuses the same record collector. It restores its wiped store from the start of the changelog, while recordCollector.offsets() still holds the last changelog offset written before the failure. If the task is closed clean before restoration finishes, that stale offset is written to the checkpoint. On the next initialization, restoration starts from that checkpoint and skips the missing records, which leaves the store empty or incomplete.

Trigger path:
1. A commit TimeoutException raises TaskCorruptedException.
2. TaskManager.handleCorruption() commits the open transaction before closing the corrupted tasks.
3. If that EndTxn times out and the commit contains no task offsets, the timeout is logged but not rethrown.
4. closeDirtyAndRevive() then calls closeDirty() on a producer that still has the pending commit.

fields.description:
The bug is that when a regex is resolved by the group coordinator, its uses the ACLs of the member that triggered the refresh. This causes an issue when the ACLs within the consumer group are not homogenous as other members could be assigned topics that they are not supposed to see. In practice, it only disclose the topic ids to those and they cannot do anything (e.g. fetching, describing) about it.

The coordinator also does not filter internal topics when resolving a regex, so the consumer config exclude.internal.topics has no effect with broker side regex (see KAFKA-21244).

Resolving it requires a KIP because we basically need to completely change the internal architecture of the regexes handling.

fields.description:
When a Streams group coordinator applies an assignment change but the heartbeat response is lost, the server and client can retain different assignments.

After a heartbeat failure, the client retries with its current active, standby, and warmup tasks. However, the server has already applied the assignment change while processing the previous request. If processing the retry produces no further assignment change, the server omits the task fields from its response. Consequently, the assignment that the client missed is not delivered again.

The following scenarios illustrate the issue. These examples use only active tasks; the client reports empty lists ({{{}[]{}}}) for standby and warmup tasks when retrying.

 

*Scenario 1: Losing an assignment response that advances the member epoch*

The client owns task {{[0]}} at member epoch {{{}1{}}}. While processing a heartbeat, the server advances the member epoch to {{2}} and assigns tasks {{{}[0, 1]{}}}, but the response is lost.

The client retries with its existing epoch {{1}} and owned task {{{}[0]{}}}. Since the server has already recorded epoch {{2}} and assignment {{{}[0, 1]{}}}, the retry response returns epoch {{2}} but omits the task fields.

The client updates its epoch to {{2}} while continuing to own only task {{{}[0]{}}}. The server considers task {{1}} assigned, but the client does not process it. This discrepancy can persist even while subsequent heartbeats succeed.

 

*Scenario 2: Losing a revocation response within the same member epoch*

The client owns tasks {{[0, 1]}} at member epoch {{{}1{}}}, and its new target assignment is {{{}[0]{}}}. The server transitions the member to {{{}UNREVOKED_TASKS{}}}, waiting for task {{1}} to be released, and responds with epoch {{1}} and the remaining task {{{}[0]{}}}. This response is lost.

Because the client did not receive the revocation instruction, it retries with epoch {{1}} and owned tasks {{{}[0, 1]{}}}. The server remains in the same state and omits the task fields because its assignment has not changed.

The client continues to own task {{1}} and cannot acknowledge its revocation. Moving that task to another member is delayed. When the existing rebalance timeout expires, the member is removed and must rejoin.

 

*Scenario 3: Losing an additional assignment within the same member epoch*

The client has already reached member epoch {{{}2{}}}, but the member is in {{{}UNRELEASED_TASKS{}}}, waiting for another member to release a task. Once the previous owner releases it, the server assigns the task without changing member epoch {{{}2{}}}. This response is lost.

The client retries with epoch {{2}} and the tasks it owned before the additional assignment. Since the server has already recorded the assignment, it omits the task fields from the retry response.

The server and client have the same member epoch but different assignments. The client does not process the task that the server considers assigned, and successful heartbeats alone may not resolve the discrepancy.

fields.description:
When Kafka Streams uses {{{}group.protocol=streams{}}}, a failure in the {{onTasksAssigned}} callback while processing a new active task assignment can leave the member unable to make further reconciliation progress.

The consumer’s partition assignment is updated before the callback runs, whereas {{currentAssignment}} is updated only after the callback succeeds. A callback failure can therefore leave the actual consumer assignment different from the last successfully reconciled assignment.

The next reconciliation attempt detects this mismatch and throws an {{{}IllegalStateException{}}}. However, {{reconciliationInProgress}} has already been set to {{{}true{}}}, and this exception path does not clear it. Subsequent attempts return immediately because they assume another reconciliation is still running.

 

*Failure scenario*

Consider a member that is successfully processing assignment A and receives a new assignment A+B:
 # Initially, both the consumer assignment and {{currentAssignment}} are A.
 # The consumer’s partition assignment is updated to A+B before invoking the assignment callback.
 # The {{onTasksAssigned}} callback throws an exception. The consumer assignment remains A+B, while {{currentAssignment}} remains A.
 # Callback failure handling clears the progress flag, allowing another reconciliation attempt to begin.
 # The next attempt sets the progress flag again, detects the mismatch between the consumer assignment and {{{}currentAssignment{}}}, and throws an exception.
 # The exception leaves the progress flag set. This blocks both retries of the same target assignment and processing of newer target assignments.

 
||Stage||Consumer Assignment||Last successufully reconciled assignment
(currentAssignment)||reconciliationInProgress||
|Initial State|A|A|false|
|New assignment applied (callback running)|A + B|A|true|
|After assignment callback failure handling|A + B|A|false|
|After the mismatch exception on the next attempt|A + B|A|true|
|Subsequent attempts|A + B|A|Remains true 
(reconciliation returns immediately)|

 

The same issue can occur when an assignment change includes revocation of existing tasks. For example, if A is revoked and the consumer assignment is changed to B before B’s assignment callback fails, the consumer assignment remains B while the completed assignment remains A. The next attempt encounters the same mismatch.

This is particularly problematic for exceptions such as {{{}TaskCorruptedException{}}}, which can be handled by an upper layer while execution continues. The membership manager can remain stuck independently of recovery from the original error.

 

*Impact*

The central issue is that an initial callback failure can escalate into a persistent state error that blocks all subsequent assignment processing.
 * *Further polling does not restore progress.* The retained progress flag prevents execution from reaching the reconciliation logic.
 * *New assignments cannot be processed.* Even if the broker provides a different target assignment, reconciliation remains blocked by the same flag.
 * *Processing of newly assigned partitions may never start while this state persists.* Partitions awaiting successful callback completion remain blocked from fetching.
 * *A live process does not imply assignment progress.* Thread execution and heartbeats may continue after error handling while reconciliation remains stalled.

As a result, even a transient or recoverable task error can prevent the member from resuming processing through subsequent assignment changes.

Subsequent attempts return immediately because they assume another reconciliation is still running.

Consider a member that is successfully processing assignment A and receives a new assignment A+B:

  1. Initially, both the consumer assignment and currentAssignment are A.
  2. The consumer’s partition assignment is updated to A+B before invoking the assignment callback.
  3. The onTasksAssigned callback throws an exception. The consumer assignment remains A+B, while currentAssignment remains A.
  4. Callback failure handling clears the progress flag, allowing another reconciliation attempt to begin.
  5. The next attempt sets the progress flag again, detects the mismatch between the consumer assignment and currentAssignment, and throws an exception.
  6. The exception leaves the progress flag set. This blocks both retries of the same target assignment and processing of newer target assignments.

 

Stage Consumer Assignment Last successufully reconciled assignment
(currentAssignment)		 reconciliationInProgress
Initial State A A false
New assignment applied (callback running) A + B A true
After assignment callback failure handling A + B A false
After the mismatch exception on the next attempt A + B A true
Subsequent attempts A + B A Remains true 
(reconciliation returns immediately)

 

The same issue can occur when an assignment change includes revocation of existing tasks. For example, if A is revoked and the consumer assignment is changed to B before B’s assignment callback fails, the consumer assignment remains B while the completed assignment remains A. The next attempt encounters the same mismatch.

This is particularly problematic for exceptions such as TaskCorruptedException, which can be handled by an upper layer while execution continues. The membership manager can remain stuck independently of recovery from the original error.

The central issue is that an initial callback failure can escalate into a persistent state error that blocks all subsequent assignment processing.

  • Further polling does not restore progress. The retained progress flag prevents execution from reaching the reconciliation logic.
  • New assignments cannot be processed. Even if the broker provides a different target assignment, reconciliation remains blocked by the same flag.
  • Processing of newly assigned partitions may never start while this state persists. Partitions awaiting successful callback completion remain blocked from fetching.
  • A live process does not imply assignment progress. Thread execution and heartbeats may continue after error handling while reconciliation remains stalled.

As a result, even a transient or recoverable task error can prevent the member from resuming processing through subsequent assignment changes.

fields.description:
We used Vagrant to run system tests on virtual machines (local or EC2), but the Docker-based runner ({{{}tests/docker/run_tests.sh{}}}) is the better choice in this area, and it is the way most of us run the system tests today. The git history shows that we update the Vagrant code only when we make another Kafka release.

In short, we should remove the {{{}Vagrantfile{}}}, {{{}vagrant/{}}}, {{{}vagrant-up.sh{}}}, and the related docs in {{tests/README.md}} to streamline our code base.

fields.description:
Our system test dependencies are hard to maintain: the S3 mirror needs manual upload, the Dockerfile and Vagrant file must be updated separately, and the Dockerfile grows by two curl lines per release.

This ticket proposes a base image on GitHub Container Registry containing the released Kafka binaries, built by a GitHub workflow after each release. Both the Dockerfile and Vagrant can pull from it, and the S3 mirror can be dropped.

fields.description:
Benchmark.test_share_consumer_throughput and Benchmark.test_producer_and_share_consumer sometimes fail with:

{code}
ValueError: could not convert string to float: ' data.consumed.in.MB'
{code}

There are three problems.

h3. 1. ShareConsumerPerformance uses --timeout as a limit for the whole run

The option is documented as "The maximum allowed time in milliseconds between returned records", and each consumer thread already follows that. But consume() waits for the threads with awaitTermination(timeout + 100ms) and then calls shutdownNow(). So the whole run can take at most timeout + 100ms, even when records are still arriving.

When the run is longer, poll() is interrupted and throws InterruptException. Since KAFKA-19450 the exception is rethrown, so the tool exits with code 1 and prints only the header line. The Python service then tries to parse the header line as numbers and fails with the ValueError above.

The tests use --timeout 20000. In a recent run, 9 of 10 measured runs took longer than 20 seconds.

h3. 2. The first share group in a cluster has to wait for __share_group_state

The __share_group_state topic (50 partitions) is created when the first share group is used. On a busy test machine this took more than 10 seconds. The consumer was already a stable member of the group, but it got no records until the topic was ready. With --timeout 20000 the consumer can give up before it reads anything.

h3. 3. The tests do not check how many records were read

The service only parses the MB and rate columns. A run that reads 0 records still passes.

With only problem 1 fixed, 5 of 10 runs passed with 0 records read.

h3. Proposed fix

* Remove the total time limit in ShareConsumerPerformance.consume() and wait for each thread. Add a unit test.
* In the two benchmark tests, read and release one record with kafka-console-share-consumer.sh before the measured run, so the share group is ready.
* In the two benchmark tests, fail if the consumers read fewer records than expected.

h3. Test results

Both tests were repeated 5 times on the kafka-e2e Jenkins job (jenkins.opensource4you.tw).

* Only the tool fix: 10 of 10 passed, but 5 runs read 0 records.
* All three fixes: 10 of 10 passed, and every run read all records.

fields.summary: getTopicEffectiveMinIsr should take the replicas from the target partition

renderedFields.description:
int getTopicEffectiveMinIsr(String topicName) {
        String minIsrConfig = configurationControl.getTopicConfig(topicName, MIN_IN_SYNC_REPLICAS_CONFIG).value();
        int currentMinIsr = Integer.parseInt(minIsrConfig);
        Uuid topicId = topicsByName.get(topicName);
        int replicationFactor = topics.get(topicId).parts.get(0).replicas.length;
        return Math.min(currentMinIsr, replicationFactor);
    }

Since each partition is allowed to have different replicas, the incorrect replica number could clear the ELR unexpectedly. For example, the first partition has only 1 replica, so the controller assumes the HW can be advanced (due to min ISR = 1) and clears the ELR set.

if (!reassignment.replicas().equals(currentReplicas)) {

The simple fix is to remove those unnecessary conditions ...

comments.body: source: https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23785/changes#r4248920995

renderedFields.description:
val valueAsString = if (isSensitive)
      null
    else value match {
      case v: String => v
      case _ => ConfigDef.convertToString(value, configEntryType.orNull)
    }

We don’t parse all broker-related values in KafkaConfig. For example, the cluster-wide and prefixed configs. Hence, we catch the “raw string” and then keep it as it is to avoid casting error.

However, we don’t even have such tests for both cases. #23785 removed the guard and CI was still green. We should add integration tests for describing a cluster-wide LIST config (e.g. log.cleanup.policy) and a prefixed LIST config (e.g. listener.name.external.ssl.enabled.protocols).
